A 5% reduction in WAL bytes likely yields 2-4% e2e lift, since the WAL bottleneck is dominated by fsync barrier rate rather than total bytes.

## Acceptance

- Empirical measurement: bench at caller_intx (today) vs committer_lazy (with persistent_staging=on, durable_queue=false at per-envelope level), K=5+warm at the optimal cell.
- Stage-timing comparison: pg_stat_statements diff to confirm enqueue-side INSERT is suppressed.
- v21 acceptance suite passes under committer_lazy + durable_queue=false (polling-based tests must still see terminal states reliably).
- Decision: either change the GUC default to committer_lazy + document the change, OR document why caller_intx must remain default and the lift is only available via explicit ALTER SYSTEM.

## Cross-refs

- Comprehensive telemetry summary: this session's measurement of acct-0sc4 baseline + WAL emitter breakdown.
- Related WAL-tuning work tracked separately (wal_compression, max_wal_size sweep).
notes:
## Measurement (clean Docker restart, K=5+warm, optimal cell)

| status_insert_mode | e2e median | CV   | submit median | drain median | avgSB |
|--------------------|-----------:|-----:|--------------:|-------------:|------:|
| caller_intx (lz4)  | 8142       | 2.6% | 9480          | 58953        | 6.8   |
| caller_intx (off)  | 8242       | 1.2% | 9513          | 60771        | 6.8   |
| committer_lazy     | **7878**   | 2.4% | 8951          | 67087        | **8.1** |

**committer_lazy regresses e2e by ~3-4% vs caller_intx.** Functional correctness OK (3/3 acceptance binaries, 9/9 tests passed under committer_lazy).

## Root cause: bottleneck shifted from WAL to staging_queue contention

pg_locks sampler wait_event histogram under each mode:

caller_intx:
  LWLock/WALWrite            278
  IO/WalSync                  44
  LWLock/poc_v21_staging_queue 13

committer_lazy:
  LWLock/poc_v21_staging_queue 185  (14x increase)
  LWLock/poc_v21_spillover_arena 6
  (WAL waits dropped below sampling threshold)

Submit phase slowed 10.51s → 11.20s (+6.5%). Drain phase slowed 60.8ms → 67.1ms avg (+10%). avgSB went 6.8 → 8.1 — committer processes larger batches per superbatch, but the increased upstream pressure on the staging queue eats the gains and then some.

Mechanism: in caller_intx, each caller's submission_status INSERT acts as an implicit rate-limiter (one fsync per envelope on the caller side). Removing it lets callers produce envelopes faster than the committer can drain them, saturating the staging_queue shmem LWLock. The new bottleneck (queue contention) is worse than the old (WAL fsync).

## pg_stat_statements diff (cumulative across 6 iters)

caller_intx (from prior session telemetry):
  20,000 calls   4,908ms  INSERT submission_status (enqueue side)
  14,490 calls   4,247ms  INSERT submission_status (Step 12 UPSERT)
  Total: 34,490 calls, 9,155ms

committer_lazy (this session):
  74,098 calls   8,971ms  INSERT submission_status (Step 12 only)
  74,098 calls     587ms  UPDATE persistent_staging (state='processing')
  74,098 calls     444ms  UPDATE persistent_staging (state='done')
  Total: 222,294 calls, 10,002ms

Eliminating the caller-side INSERT did NOT reduce total submission_status work — Step 12 calls 5x more frequently in committer_lazy (12,350/iter vs 14,490/run in caller_intx — about the same per-iter actually, ~14k each), so the savings are roughly cancelled by the new persistent_staging UPDATEs.

## Decision: keep caller_intx as default

Reasoning:
1. committer_lazy regresses throughput on this workload (-3.4% e2e).
2. The implicit-throttle property of caller_intx is workload-protective: without per-caller fsync pacing, the staging queue saturates.
3. Mode is operationally correct (acceptance tests pass) — flip is available for workloads where caller-side INSERT is hot but the committer has headroom.

Future revisit: committer_lazy MAY become a win after either (a) larger drain_batch_size with proven committer headroom, (b) wider committer parallelism (committer_count > 1, also tracked separately), or (c) larger staging_queue_size if observed contention is transient burst not steady-state.

## Updated bench ceiling

Clean Docker restart + committed optimization stack (a2sj/ed7u/0sc4) + current config (wal_compression=lz4, status_insert_mode=caller_intx, batch_window_us=500):

**~8200 evps median, CV 1-2%**

This is ~+15% above the prior session's '7180' baseline number, which was contaminated by host CPU load (Chrome ~50% during measurement).
close_reason: committer_lazy regresses e2e by 3.4% on this workload — bottleneck shifts from caller-side WAL fsync to staging_queue LWLock contention. Functional correctness verified (acceptance tests pass). Keeping caller_intx default. See notes for measurement + mechanism.

title: committer Step 3: pre-hydrate or cache standard_costs / avg_pool_state lookups
description:
## Context

acct-pl3b stage-timing: pre_apply is 1297 µs/SB (38.6% of pipeline). Step 3 (snapshot hydration) is one component. For std cost, Step 3 runs hydrate_standard_costs which issues a single SELECT FROM poc_v21_standard_costs WHERE sku_id = ANY(...) per SB.

## Problem

For workloads with stable cost configurations (the common case), standard_costs rows don't change SB-to-SB. Re-reading them per SB is wasted SPI work. Same applies to avg_pool_state (for avg cost method).

Currently committer.rs::hydrate_standard_costs runs once per SB, ~50-100 µs even for warm shared_buffers. avg_pool_state via hydrate_avg_pools is similar.

## Proposed Change

Add a process-local hydration cache per committer worker, keyed by (sku_id, location_id) → standard_cost (or avg_pool_state):

1. On Step 3, check cache for each pool key in the SB
2. Only un-cached keys go to the SELECT
3. Populate cache from SELECT results
4. Invalidate cache on: (a) ALTER on standard_costs (catalog event hook), (b) bench reset, (c) bounded LRU eviction at 16384 entries

For avg_pool_state — every drain MUTATES avg_pool_state, so cache must be updated locally after Step 5e UPSERT.

For standard_costs — mostly read-only at runtime. Standard cost rolls are batch operations done via post_standard_cost_roll (rare). A simple per-worker cache with cache TTL of 60s is probably enough.

## Expected Impact

Step 3 hydration is probably ~100-200 µs/SB. Caching it could drop to ~5 µs (HashMap lookup). ~10% pre_apply reduction = ~3-5% e2e lift.

Predicted new e2e: ~4400-4500 evps at optimal config (modest, since Step 3 is one of four pre_apply components).

## Acceptance

- Code change: committer.rs adds CostCache struct per worker, used in hydrate_standard_costs / hydrate_avg_pools
- All acceptance tests pass (especially: tests that update standard_costs mid-run see the new value)
- Bench at optimal config — expect e2e >= 4400 evps
- Stage-timing reports pre_apply reduced 5-10%

## Risks

- Cache staleness: standard_cost rolls happen via post_standard_cost_roll in production. The cache must invalidate. TTL is simplest but causes brief stale reads. Catalog-event invalidation is correct but complex.
- avg_pool_state mutability: cache must be write-through (update local cache after Step 5e). Bugs here cause silent cost drift.
- Multi-worker: each worker has its own cache. Cost rolls land in PG, but only the first SB per worker sees it. Acceptable for std (rare rolls); concerning for avg (mutates per drain — workers see local writes, no cross-worker share).

## Cross-refs

- Stacks with Step 2 pool_locks cache (separate issue)
- Independent of Step 5 bulk_insert optimizations
close_reason:
Shipped as 9c91e8b. Process-local HashMap<(sku, loc), unit_cost> per worker caches Step 3 standard_costs hydration; invalidation via new public pg_extern poc_v21_invalidate_committer_caches() that fetch_adds a shmem AtomicU64 version counter (anyone mutating poc_v21_standard_costs must call it). Worker compares its last-known version against shmem each hydrate; mismatch clears cache.

Wired into the 5 test/bench seed sites that INSERT into standard_costs: tests/common/mod.rs, tests/common/m8_runner.rs, tests/common/m82_statistical.rs, tests/bench_m8_ceiling.rs, tests/acceptance_v21_enqueue_batch.rs.

AVG cache deliberately not implemented — avg_pool_state mutates per-drain; cross-worker stale window has no cheap detection signal.

Measurement at optimal cell (count=100k, spread=100, normal, ib=5, rsb=5000, N=8, drain_batch=2, K=7+warm):

  stage           baseline    ed7u      delta
  parse            107876     79503    -26%
  pre_apply       1142338    788002    -31%   <-- target 5-10%, exceeded
  apply             15868     14888     -6%
  bulk_insert      835667    807017     -3%
  post             558124    534039     -4%
  pipeline_total  2556004   2148985    -16%

  e2e_evps median   6571      7182    +9.3%   <-- target 3-5%, exceeded

Caveat: this measurement was taken with Chrome at ~53% CPU; baseline pre_apply (1142k) was somewhat noise-inflated relative to clean-system recall (~1038k). The 31% pre_apply delta likely overstates the per-call savings; e2e +9.3% is the load-bearing number. One ed7u iter hit a 744 evps outlier (mean 5995 vs median 7182) — median is robust.

v21 acceptance suite: 30 green / 2 known-flaky (router_groups_transitive, router_recovery — both documented parallel-spawn races, pass on retry, unrelated to this change).

title: committer Step 2: cache pool_locks INSERT — skip when row exists (pre_apply 38.6% target)
description:
## Context

acct-pl3b stage-timing: pre_apply is 1297 µs/SB (38.6% of pipeline). pre_apply spans Step 2 (lex-lock acquisition), Step 2.45 (caller-tx coupling check), Step 2.5 (within-SB cross-envelope dedup), and Step 3 (snapshot hydration). Step 2 has two SPI calls:

1. INSERT INTO poc_v21_pool_locks (sku_id, location_id) SELECT ... FROM UNNEST ... ON CONFLICT (sku_id, location_id) DO NOTHING
2. SELECT 1 FROM poc_v21_pool_locks WHERE (sku_id, location_id) IN (...) FOR UPDATE

The INSERT step exists to ensure a row exists for each pool key before the FOR UPDATE can succeed. Once a pool has been touched once, the row stays in poc_v21_pool_locks forever. So the INSERT is almost always a no-op — but it still costs PG planning + execution + WAL (even ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING writes a 0-byte WAL marker per non-conflicting row).

## Problem

For long-running systems where every pool has been seen at least once, the Step 2 INSERT is pure overhead. ~50-100 µs per SB wasted.

## Proposed Change

Add a process-local pool_locks_seen cache (HashSet<(i64,i64)>) per committer worker. On Step 2:

1. Filter the SB's pool keys against the cache — only un-seen keys go to the INSERT
2. Run the INSERT only for the residual (probably empty after warmup)
3. SELECT FOR UPDATE on the full set (cache hit pool keys still need the FOR UPDATE)
4. On INSERT success, add the keys to the cache

Cache eviction: bounded LRU (e.g., 16384 entries) — covers all hot pools easily.

For correctness: if the cache says 'seen' but the row got deleted (admin TRUNCATE, recon clean-up), the FOR UPDATE will return 0 rows → re-INSERT path triggers. Add a fallback.

## Expected Impact

For warm caches: ~70-100 µs/SB savings. ~5% pre_apply reduction = ~2-3% e2e lift on its own.

For cold caches (first N SBs): no impact. For tests / restarts: re-warm in <100 SBs.

Predicted new e2e: ~4350-4400 evps at optimal config.

## Acceptance

- Code change: committer.rs Step 2 checks cache before INSERT
- All acceptance tests pass (including the 'pool_locks row gets deleted mid-flight' edge case)
- Bench at optimal config (with bench setup populating the cache): expect e2e >= 4350 evps
- Stage-timing reports pre_apply reduced 3-7%

## Risks

- Stale cache after admin cleanup of pool_locks: FOR UPDATE returns 0 rows. Need fallback to re-INSERT-and-retry.
- Multi-worker: each worker has its own cache. First SB per worker hits the slow path. Negligible for steady-state.
- Cache growth: bounded LRU prevents unbounded memory growth.

## Cross-refs

- Stacks with other pre_apply optimizations (Step 3 hydration cache — separate issue)
- Lower-impact than Step 5 work but cheap to implement
close_reason:
Shipped as afcb3c3. Process-local HashSet caches per worker (cap 16k, clear-on-overflow) skip the Step 2 INSERT for known-present pool keys. FOR UPDATE wraps in SELECT count(*) for stale-cache detection — row-count shortfall triggers re-INSERT + retry.

Measurement at optimal cell (count=100k, spread=100, normal, ib=5, rsb=5000, N=8, drain_batch=2, K=5+warm):

  stage           baseline    a2sj      delta
  parse              92907    92637    -0.3%
  pre_apply        1091881  1037572    -5.0%   <-- target met (3-7%)
  apply              14410    14332    -0.5%
  bulk_insert       760571   751300    -1.2%
  post              511352   512180    +0.2%
  pipeline_total   2381894  2327511    -2.3%

  e2e_evps median     6913     6990    +1.1%

Pre_apply 5.0% reduction is in the issue's predicted 3-7% band. e2e
lift (+1.1%) is under the predicted 2-3% — pre_apply is ~46% of
pipeline_total so a 5% pre_apply move only carries ~2% to pipeline,
and bulk_insert/post are still ~46% combined unrelated to this work.

NOTE on baseline correction: the post-6kcx pre-compaction memo
claimed e2e median ~7376; today's true HEAD baseline at the same
optimal cell is ~6913 (CV 0.2%). The 7376 number was from a
different docker session and the recall didn't survive. The
delta-direction conclusions in this session are based on the
6913 baseline measured today.

v21 acceptance suite: 32/32 green.

title: committer pipeline: batch multiple SuperBatches into one drain transaction
description:
## Context

acct-pl3b stage-timing: total pipeline is 3362 µs/SB, dominated by bulk_insert + pre_apply (84%). Each SB is its own sub-transaction (savepoint) inside the committer BGWorker's outer transaction. Per-SB cost includes WAL group commit setup, txn ID allocation, pg_xact bit setting, and (if config requires) fsync.

## Problem

The committer drains one SB per pipeline iteration. At avgSB=7.9 envelopes/SB, each pipeline iteration writes ~24 rows total but pays full per-txn overhead. WAL commit cost (group commit eligible) and pg_xact bits per sub-txn don't amortize across SBs even though they share the outer transaction.

## Proposed Change

Drain N (configurable, e.g. 4) SBs in one pipeline iteration, all under ONE sub-transaction:

1. Outer loop: dequeue up to N SBs from CommitterQueue
2. Open ONE sub-transaction
3. For each SB: parse + Step 2 + Step 2.5 + Step 3 + Step 4 + Step 5 + Step 12
4. ReleaseCurrentSubTransaction
5. Step 14 cleanup for all N SBs

Within the sub-txn, the lex-locks (Step 2) for SB[i] are still acquired in order — but the lock set is the UNION of all N SBs' pool keys.

Considerations:
- One bad SB rolls back ALL N (failure isolation regression). Need a 'failure splitter': on rollback, retry the N SBs each in their own sub-txn to localize the failure.
- Lex-lock conflict: if SB[1] and SB[3] need the same pool key, they're already serialized at the queue level. Within one sub-txn they need to be ordered.
- WAL commit: PG group commits transactions that arrive together. Multiple committer workers running in parallel already give group commit some hits. Batching within one worker may not stack with that, but reduces per-worker txn count.

## Expected Impact

If per-SB pipeline cost has a fixed overhead of ~500 µs (WAL setup + xact + status row), batching 4 SBs amortizes that to 125 µs/SB. ~10-15% e2e lift IF txn overhead is the right fraction. Could be more if WAL commit dominates.

Predicted new e2e: ~5000-5500 evps at optimal config.

## Acceptance

- Code change: committer.rs adds a batch_size GUC + drain loop that bundles up to N SBs
- All acceptance tests pass — especially failure-isolation tests (single bad envelope still surfaces correctly via the rollback-and-retry path)
- Bench at optimal config — expect e2e >= 5000 evps
- Stage-timing reports per-SB pipeline ns reduced ~15-25%

## Risks

- Failure-isolation regression: one bad SB rolls back the bundle. Need the retry-split path.
- Lock duration: holding the union of N SBs' pool locks for longer increases contention with other committers and with caller-tx events.
- WAL record size: one txn with 4× rows means 4× larger WAL record. Approaches wal_buffers segment boundary at ~7-15 SBs — could force intermediate flushes mid-txn.
- Status UPSERT: 4 SBs worth of status rows in one statement is fine; just bigger.

## Cross-refs

- Orthogonal to bulk_insert optimizations (acct-xwu3 / gfvb / meov / COPY) — stacks multiplicatively
- May reduce the value of CTE-merge (gfvb) since the SPI roundtrip overhead amortizes naturally
close_reason: Shipped: poc_v21.drain_batch_size GUC, default 2. Outer loop in poc_v21_committer_main bundles up to N claims under one BackgroundWorker::transaction; each SB still runs in its own internal sub-tx for per-pipeline failure isolation. Measured under acct-rq4w methodology (K=5+warm) at optimal config: N=2 gives e2e median 7376 vs baseline 5338 (+38%, CV 2.0%, clean). N=4 captures similar median but 1/5 iters hit 120s drain timeout from pool_locks lex-lock contention — picked N=2 as safer + measured-best default. Pipeline_total reduced 12.5% (2091→1830 µs/SB). All correctness tests pass including failure isolation. Commit 7add223.

title: committer Step 5: COPY FROM via in-memory tuple stream — alternative bulk-load path
description:
## Context

acct-pl3b stage-timing: bulk_insert at 1529 µs/SB (45.5% of pipeline). Sibling proposal acct-meov pursues heap_multi_insert FFI. This issue tracks the COPY FROM alternative.

## Problem

PG's COPY FROM is the highest-level bulk-load primitive in PG. It bypasses parsing INSERTs, planner, and executor — handles tuple stream directly to heap_multi_insert internally + index update. Latency-per-row is 3-5× lower than INSERT.

## Proposed Change

Implement Step 5 INSERTs via the COPY FROM protocol from extension code:

1. Build an in-memory binary-format COPY stream (PG's binary format is well-documented; header + per-row tuple bytes)
2. Call BeginCopyFrom() with a PG_RECEIVER_KIND_INTERNAL receiver that reads from the buffer
3. Loop NextCopyFrom() until exhausted
4. EndCopyFrom()

Equivalent: implement a CustomTableSlotsBuilder that COPY's machinery accepts and feed it slots in batch.

Per-table bulk path: posting_lines, cost_layers, posting_line_inventory each get their own COPY stream.

## Expected Impact

Same order as heap_multi_insert FFI (~30-40% e2e lift) — they share the underlying primitive. COPY adds binary-format serialization overhead but skips planner/executor.

Predicted new e2e: ~6000 evps at optimal config.

## Acceptance

- Code change: COPY-protocol streaming helper in committer.rs
- All acceptance tests pass
- Bench at optimal config — expect e2e >= 6000 evps
- Stage-timing reports bulk_insert reduced by 40-60%

## Risks

- Binary COPY format is endian-sensitive and PG-version-tied. PG 18 has specific header bytes.
- Type encoders (bigint, jsonb, uuid, timestamptz, xid8, numeric) each need their binary encoders implemented. pgrx may provide some.
- Triggers + index update still need to be invoked (COPY does call them; FFI heap_multi_insert doesn't).
- BIGSERIAL allocation: same problem as heap_multi_insert — needs explicit nextval handling.
- Returning IDs: COPY FROM doesn't have RETURNING. Either pre-assign via nextval(N) or refactor downstream to not need IDs.

## Cross-refs

- Alternative to acct-meov (heap_multi_insert direct FFI) — pick one path based on prototype results
- Both subsume the CTE-merge (acct-gfvb) and RETURNING-drop (acct-y1ci) wins
- Compare/contrast via micro-prototype before committing to one
notes:
## Deferral 2026-05-20

Investigated post-6kcx and found that the issue's amortization premise was wrong. Re-reading the pre-implementation analysis: it assumed 6kcx would aggregate row counts per Step 5 INSERT call to 32-64 rows. What 6kcx actually did: wrap N `process_superbatch` calls in one outer `BackgroundWorker::transaction`. Each `process_superbatch` still runs its OWN Step 5 sequence as a sub-tx — so per-call row count is unchanged at ~8 rows (one SB's worth).

At 8 rows/call, COPY's setup cost (~150µs BeginCopyFrom + state alloc + options parse + open trigger info) loses to the current bulk INSERT-via-UNNEST (~100µs). Also: posting_lines and cost_layers use RETURNING for downstream linking (posting_line_id → inventory; layer_id → depletion), and COPY doesn't have RETURNING — switching to nextval pre-allocation adds another SPI roundtrip.

Path to actually win 83oq: implement cross-SB Step 5 aggregation — defer the non-RETURNING tables (cost_depletions, cost_consumptions, posting_line_inventory, avg_pool_state UPSERT) into thread-local buffers across the drain batch, flush once via COPY at the end of the outer transaction. Steps 5a (posting_lines INSERT RETURNING) and 5b (cost_layers INSERT RETURNING) still have to run per-SB because subsequent within-SB steps depend on the returned IDs.

That restructure is invasive (touches the entire Step 5 sequencing model) and the predicted gain on top of current performance is modest — bulk_insert is now 807µs ≈ 38% of pipeline, ~40% bulk_insert win = ~6% e2e at best. Risk/reward unfavorable.

Reopened. Pickup conditions: either a workload measurement shows avgSB substantially > 8 (which would naturally push COPY into its winning regime without restructuring), or a deliberate Step 5 cross-SB aggregation epic is scoped that bundles 83oq with the prerequisite refactor.

Status reverted to open.

title: committer Step 5: heap_multi_insert via FFI — bypass PG executor for bulk INSERTs
description:
## Context

acct-pl3b stage-timing shows bulk_insert at 1529 µs/SB (45.5% of pipeline) for std cost po_receipt at avgSB=7.9 envelopes. Current implementation uses INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM UNNEST(...) via SPI — the PG planner + executor runs every batch.

## Problem

PG's executor adds overhead vs the bare 'write rows to heap' primitive. COPY FROM uses heap_multi_insert directly to bypass the executor and achieve 3-5× the raw INSERT throughput. extension code can call heap_multi_insert from C/Rust FFI for the same speedup, but with full WAL + index updates preserved.

## Proposed Change

Implement Step 5 bulk INSERTs via direct heap_multi_insert FFI calls instead of SPI INSERT ... SELECT.

Outline:
1. For each target table, prepare a Vec<TupleTableSlot> populated with the row values (using PG's slot APIs)
2. Acquire the table's heap relation (table_open with NoLock since the txn already holds it)
3. Call heap_multi_insert(rel, slots, n, cid, options, bistate) — single C call writes N tuples to heap pages, generates WAL records in one buffer
4. Call ExecInsertIndexTuples per slot for each index (this is what the executor would do; can't be skipped without losing index consistency)
5. table_close

For tables with RETURNING (5a posting_lines, 5b cost_layers): use heap_multi_insert which populates ItemPointer in each slot, then read tts_tid to recover the assigned BIGSERIAL — except BIGSERIAL is a sequence, not derived from TID. May need to bulk-allocate sequence values via nextval(sequence_name) loop separately, then put them in slots.

## Expected Impact

3-5× reduction in bulk_insert time. ~1000 µs/SB savings = ~30% pipeline reduction = ~30-40% e2e lift.

Predicted new e2e: ~6000-6500 evps at optimal config.

## Acceptance

- Code change: new committer.rs helper that takes Vec<RowStruct> and writes via heap_multi_insert
- 5a + 5b + 5d use the new helper; 5c/5c'/5e migrate over time
- All acceptance tests pass — especially conformance tests that check posting_line shape, cost_layers correctness, inventory shape
- Bench at optimal config — expect e2e >= 6000 evps
- Stage-timing reports bulk_insert reduced by 50-70%

## Risks

- HUGE: heap_multi_insert is a low-level PG internal. Misuse corrupts heap or skips WAL. Easy to get wrong.
- Index update must run separately per row — heap_multi_insert doesn't do it. Implementation needs ExecInsertIndexTuples loop.
- Triggers (BEFORE/AFTER INSERT, statement-level) are NOT fired by heap_multi_insert. If any of the 5 tables grows triggers we'd silently skip them.
- BIGSERIAL value allocation: need nextval('seq', N) — PG has setval but not direct bulk allocation. Likely requires sequence cache or explicit nextval loop.
- pgrx 0.18 may not expose heap_multi_insert directly — needs raw pg_sys bindings + unsafe wrapping.

## Cross-refs

- Alternative path: COPY FROM (separate issue) — same primitive, different API
- Lower-risk first step: skip dead-weight INSERTs (acct-xwu3), CTE-merge (acct-gfvb)
- Pre-requisite: those should land first so the heap_multi_insert work is on a smaller surface
close_reason: Feasibility investigation showed scope larger than the issue outlined: posting_line_inventory's FK constraint on posting_lines creates internal RI triggers (tgisinternal=TRUE) that heap_multi_insert does NOT fire. Correct implementation requires ExecARInsertTriggers + AfterTriggerSaveEvent + ExecInsertIndexTuples + bulk nextval pre-alloc — substantial unsafe FFI surface. Plus post-xwu3 bulk_insert is now 702 µs/SB (not the pl3b-era 1529 µs the issue estimated against), shrinking the realistic gain ceiling to ~10-15% e2e instead of 30-40%. acct-83oq (COPY FROM) uses the same heap_multi_insert primitive underneath but PG's COPY plumbing handles FK RI + indexes + serial allocation correctly — dramatically smaller risk surface for similar gain ceiling. Redirecting to 83oq.

title: committer Step 5: CTE-merge remaining INSERTs into single SPI call
description:
## Context

acct-pl3b stage-timing showed bulk_insert at 1529 µs/SB (45.5% of pipeline). Step 5 currently does 2-6 separate SPI roundtrips for the bulk INSERTs (5a posting_lines, 5b cost_layers, 5c cost_depletions, 5c' cost_consumptions, 5d posting_line_inventory, 5e avg_pool_state) — each is its own Spi::connect → select → execute cycle.

## Problem

Each Spi::connect has fixed overhead (~50-100µs measured elsewhere in pgrx benchmarks). For 3 active INSERTs in std cost, that's ~150-300µs of pure roundtrip overhead, even before INSERT work. CTE merging into one SPI call collapses all roundtrips to one.

## Proposed Change

Combine the active INSERTs into a single `WITH ... INSERT ... RETURNING ...` statement:

```sql
WITH ins_pl AS (
  INSERT INTO poc_v21_posting_lines (...)
  SELECT ... FROM UNNEST(...)
  RETURNING posting_line_id, ordinal_marker
),
ins_cl AS (
  INSERT INTO poc_v21_cost_layers (...)
  SELECT ... FROM UNNEST(...)
  RETURNING layer_id, correlation_id
),
ins_pli AS (
  INSERT INTO poc_v21_posting_line_inventory (...)
  SELECT (SELECT posting_line_id FROM ins_pl WHERE ordinal_marker = t.ordinal),
         (SELECT layer_id FROM ins_cl WHERE correlation_id = t.corr),
         t.sku_id, t.location_id, t.qty
    FROM UNNEST(...) AS t(ordinal, corr, sku_id, location_id, qty)
)
SELECT 1;
```

This requires marker columns (ordinal_marker, correlation_id) on the RETURNING rows so the downstream INSERTs can join back. Currently the Rust side does this join post-hoc by index — moving it to SQL CTE means SQL planner handles the link.

## Expected Impact

Saves ~100-200 µs per SB (2 SPI roundtrip eliminations). Smaller wins on uniform_1000 (each INSERT had fewer rows). ~5-10% bulk_insert reduction = ~3-5% e2e lift.

Predicted new e2e: ~4400-4500 evps at optimal config (smaller than skip-dead-weight).

## Acceptance

- Code change: replace 3-6 separate Spi::connect calls in committer.rs Step 5 with one CTE
- All acceptance tests pass
- Re-run pl3b_sweep optimal config — expect e2e >= 4400 evps
- Stage-timing reports bulk_insert avg_ns reduced by 5-15%

## Risks

- CTE planner may decide to materialize differently than expected; benchmark the actual rowcounts via EXPLAIN
- Error paths get harder to localize: with separate INSERTs an SQLSTATE pinpoints which one failed; with CTE the whole stmt rolls back
- Mixing INSERTs with different conflict modes (some have ON CONFLICT, others don't) is awkward — may need to keep some separate

## Cross-refs

- Stacks ON acct-pl3b-skip-cost-layers (if cost_layers is removed for std, the CTE becomes 2-INSERT instead of 3)
- Alternative: heap_multi_insert FFI (lower-level, larger win)
notes:
## Re-measured under acct-rq4w methodology (K=5 + warmup, CV ~1%)

Implementation: WITH ins AS (INSERT posting_lines ... RETURNING posting_line_id, correlation_id, sub_priority), inv AS (INSERT posting_line_inventory ... JOIN ins ON (correlation_id, sub_priority) RETURNING 1) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM inv. Single Spi::connect, 18 params.

Required reordering Step 5: 5b cost_layers → 5c depletions → 5c' consumptions → merged 5a+5d CTE → 5e avg_pool_state. This is because the merged CTE consumes new_layer_ids_by_corr (populated by 5b) when building the inventory layer_id column.

### Measurement (optimal config: spread=100 normal, ib=5, rsb_max=5000, N=8, committer_lazy, N=100k, K=5+warm)

| metric                | baseline (pre-gfvb) | gfvb v2  | delta  | significance |
|-----------------------|--------------------:|---------:|-------:|--------------|
| e2e median (evps)     |                5338 |     5437 | +1.9%  | borderline (t≈2.3, p≈0.05) |
| e2e mean              |                5349 |     5431 | +1.5%  |              |
| e2e CV                |                1.2% |     0.9% | (both low) |          |
| pipeline_total/SB µs  |                2091 |     1998 | -4.4%  | clear (~3σ)  |
| bulk_insert/SB µs     |                 702 |      729 | +3.8%  | small regression |
| pre_apply/SB µs       |                 987 |      881 | -10.7% | suspicious gain (cross-run variance?) |
| post/SB µs            |                 378 |      368 | -2.6%  |              |
| parse/SB µs           |                 427 |      434 | +1.6%  | noise        |
| apply/SB µs           |                  15 |       14 | -7%    | tiny absolute |

### Findings

1. **bulk_insert specifically got worse (+3.8%)**: the multi-INSERT CTE planning + composite-key JOIN cost exceeds the saved SPI roundtrip overhead at our SB size (~8 envelopes/SB). The original hypothesis "one Spi::connect saves ~100µs/SB" is contradicted at the bulk_insert stage.

2. **pre_apply improvement is suspicious**: gfvb only touches Step 5; pre_apply is Steps 2/2.45/2.5/3 (snapshot hydration). A 10.7% drop is too large for direct causation. Plausible explanations:
   - PG internal state churn from fewer SPI calls bleeds into next-SB pre_apply
   - Cross-run environmental variance even with warmup (different OS scheduler load, autovacuum, etc.)
   - Within-run CV is 0.9% but between-run pre_apply variance might be higher; would need alternating baseline/gfvb runs to control

3. **The e2e win (+1.9%) is real but small AND load-bearing on the suspicious pre_apply gain**. If pre_apply's improvement is environmental, the true e2e effect of gfvb is closer to 0 or slightly negative.

### Decision: REVERT

The signal is too weak to justify added complexity:
- +1.9% e2e at p≈0.05 isn't a decisive win
- The bulk_insert regression (+3.8%) is directionally bad and the stated mechanism of the win
- Added complexity: 18 params instead of 12+5; composite-key JOIN; harder to localize SQL errors; longer prepared-statement plan

Filing as "investigated, real but marginal, not merging" rather than closing as won/lost. The CTE shape is a known reachable optimization if a future change makes the savings more material (e.g., if SBs grow much larger and the per-call PG overhead matters more).

### Future work

If revisiting: alternate baseline/gfvb runs (5+5) and t-test the differences directly to control for environmental drift. Also worth measuring at avgSB=50+ where per-call SPI overhead amortizes differently and the CTE planner cost amortizes too.

Commit history: applied at d891138-d (pre-revert), reverted before commit. Bench commit: 91021c4 (rq4w methodology).
close_reason: Investigated under acct-rq4w methodology (K=5+warm, CV ~1%). Result: +1.9% e2e median lift at p≈0.05 (borderline), but bulk_insert specifically regressed +3.8% and the e2e win was load-bearing on a suspicious -10.7% pre_apply gain that gfvb shouldn't directly affect. The CTE planning overhead at SB=8 exceeds the SPI-roundtrip savings. Reverted; not merging at our current SB sizes. See issue notes for full measurement table + reasons. Reachable optimization if a future change makes SBs much larger; until then, complexity not justified.

title: committer Step 5: skip cost_layers INSERT for std cost (dead-weight rows)
description:
## Context

After acct-pl3b shipped + sweep + stage-timing instrumentation, the v2.1 single-machine e2e ceiling is 4533 evps at the optimal config (spread=100 normal, ingress_batch=5, N=8, committer_lazy). Stage-timing breakdown at that config (avg per SuperBatch, avgSB=7.9 envelopes):

| stage          | avg ns/SB | %     |
|----------------|----------:|------:|
| parse          | 434 µs    | 12.9% |
| pre_apply      | 1297 µs   | 38.6% |
| apply          | 22 µs     | 0.7%  |
| **bulk_insert**| **1529 µs**| **45.5%** |
| post           | 506 µs    | 15.0% |
| TOTAL          | 3362 µs/SB| 100%  |

Step 5 has 6 conditional INSERTs (posting_lines, cost_layers, cost_depletions, cost_consumptions, posting_line_inventory, avg_pool_state). For std cost po_receipt only 3 actually fire (5a posting_lines, 5b cost_layers, 5d posting_line_inventory) — the other 3 are empty-vec gated and skip cleanly.

## Problem

Of the 3 INSERTs that fire for std cost, **cost_layers (5b) is dead-weight**: std cost does not deplete layers (depletions go through avg_pool_state or are absent for std). No downstream consumer reads cost_layers rows born from std method. The INSERT path runs because src/standard.rs::apply_one (lines 127-150 in current HEAD) unconditionally pushes a PocV21LayerRow regardless of method.

## Proposed Change

1. Add a method-aware skip at the standard.rs apply_one's receive() path: do NOT push to result.layer_inserts when the SKU's resolved cost method is 'std'.
2. Optionally keep pool.layers in-memory tracking (for snapshot bookkeeping consistency, line 142) — that's free.
3. Verify no downstream PG query references cost_layers rows where source_kind='po_receipt' AND the parent SKU is std-method.

## Expected Impact

If cost_layers is 1 of 3 actual INSERTs (~510 µs of the 1529 µs bulk_insert), skipping it = ~33% bulk_insert reduction = ~15% pipeline reduction = ~10-15% e2e lift.

Predicted new e2e: ~4900-5100 evps at optimal config.

## Acceptance

- Code change: standard.rs::receive() skips result.layer_inserts.push() and pool.layers.push() when method=='std'
- All acceptance tests still pass (run scripts/run-tests-v21.sh)
- Re-run pl3b_sweep at config (spread=100, normal, ib=5, rsb=5000, N=8, committer_lazy) — expect e2e >= 4900 evps
- Stage-timing reports bulk_insert reduced by 25-35%
- Recon check: no orphaned references to std-source cost_layers from any other table

## Risks

- If any audit/recon SQL implicitly expects ONE cost_layer per receipt, that query needs updating. Search for cost_layers JOIN/WHERE before merging.
- The snapshot's pool.layers Vec tracking is currently used for FIFO depletion — std doesn't deplete, so removing the push there is safe.

## Cross-refs

- Parent finding: acct-pl3b sweep results (commit 70240f9, bench/results-m8-ceiling/pl3b-sweep/)
- Alternative paths: cte-merge (separate issue), heap_multi_insert FFI (separate issue), COPY FROM (separate issue)
close_reason: STD PoReceipt/InvAdjust skip the dead-weight cost_layers INSERT; WoComplete-output STD audit layer preserved via emit_layer=true. Measured e2e 4533→5088 evps (+12%), bulk_insert/SB 1529→773 µs (-49%), pipeline total/SB 3362→2257 µs (-33%) at optimal config (spread=100 normal, ib=5, rsb_max=5000, N=8, committer_lazy, N=100k). Commit d891138.

title: denormalize cost_layers.effective_qty: eliminate correlated subquery in FIFO hydration
description: Shortcut B from acct-hg9g audit. Today's hydrate_fifo_layers query computes effective_qty per layer via a correlated subquery on cost_depletions. Replace with a denormalized cost_layers.effective_qty column maintained at depletion-write time. Eliminates the O(N²) shape; hydration becomes O(touched_layers). Win is independent of whether the SB has depletions — applies any time hydration is needed.
acceptance_criteria: ALTER TABLE poc_v21_cost_layers ADD COLUMN effective_qty BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0. Step 5c (cost_depletions INSERT) also runs UPDATE cost_layers SET effective_qty = effective_qty - depleted_qty WHERE layer_id = . hydrate_fifo_layers query drops the correlated subquery, selects effective_qty directly. All existing FIFO tests pass. Bench regression: FIFO depletion workload should see lower pipeline_ns_per_drain on hot pools.

title: committer shortcut audit: (event × cost_method) matrix and per-cell work shortcuts
description:
Meta-audit of what the committer actually NEEDS per (event, cost_method) cell vs what it DOES today. Triggered by acct-cyu6 finding that FIFO + pure-receipt batches paid O(N²) hydration tax for nothing.

## What each apply_one actually reads

**FIFO** (`src/fifo.rs::apply_one`):
- Receipt (qty>0; po_receipt, inv_adjust+, wo_complete output): calls `emit_layer` — pushes a new LayerView onto pool.layers (bookkeeping for the eventual Step 5b INSERT). **Does NOT read pool.layers existing contents.**
- Depletion (qty<0; inv_issue, so_shipment, scrap, wo_complete component, inv_adjust−, op_move source): calls `deplete` — reads pool.layers sorted by (born_at, born_seq), walks oldest-first. **NEEDS hydration.**
- qty==0 inv_adjust: emits amount=0 posting line. **NEEDS nothing.**

**AVG** (`src/avg.rs::apply_one`):
- Receipt: calls `roll_in` — reads pool.avg_unit_cost + pool.avg_total_qty to roll the weighted average. **NEEDS hydration.**
- Depletion: calls `consume` — reads pool.avg_unit_cost. **NEEDS hydration.**
- qty==0: audit-only. NEEDS nothing.

**STD** (`src/standard.rs::apply_one`):
- Receipt (po_receipt, inv_adjust+): reads snapshot.standard_costs[(sku, loc)]. **NEEDS hydration (1 row per pool).**
- Depletion: same lookup. **NEEDS hydration.**
- WoComplete output (qty>0): emits at event.unit_cost (caller-supplied = dispatcher-computed component cost roll-up). **Does NOT read standard_costs.**
- qty==0: NEEDS nothing.

## Matrix: what work does Step 3 hydration ACTUALLY need to do per cell

| event_kind | direction | FIFO | AVG | STD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| po_receipt | receipt | **NONE** | row per pool | row per pool |
| inv_adjust qty>0 | receipt | **NONE** | row per pool | row per pool |
| inv_adjust qty<0 | depletion | layer list | row per pool | row per pool |
| inv_adjust qty=0 | audit | **NONE** | **NONE** | **NONE** |
| inv_issue | depletion | layer list | row per pool | row per pool |
| so_shipment | depletion | layer list | row per pool | row per pool |
| scrap | depletion | layer list | row per pool | row per pool |
| wo_complete component | depletion | layer list | row per pool | row per pool |
| wo_complete output | receipt | **NONE** | row per pool | **NONE** (uses event.unit_cost) |
| op_move source | depletion | layer list | row per pool | row per pool |
| op_move dest | receipt | **NONE** | row per pool | row per pool |

## What Step 3 does today

`process_superbatch` Step 3 unconditionally hydrates per method:
- All FIFO pools touched → `hydrate_fifo_layers` (selects from cost_layers with correlated subquery per row on cost_depletions)
- All AVG pools touched → `hydrate_avg_pools` (selects 1 row per pool from avg_pool_state)
- All STD pools touched → `hydrate_standard_costs` (selects 1 row per pool from standard_costs)

This is eager. No event inspection. No "skip if no event reads this state."

## Shortcuts identified

### A. FIFO + no depletions in SB → skip `hydrate_fifo_layers`
Already filed as **acct-00na**. The big win for receipt-only FIFO workloads (PO arrivals, returns, positive adjustments).

### B. Denormalize `cost_layers.effective_qty`
When FIFO hydration IS needed, the current SQL has a correlated subquery per layer:

```sql
SELECT ..., (qty - COALESCE((SELECT SUM(qty) FROM cost_depletions d 
                              WHERE d.layer_id = cost_layers.layer_id), 0))::bigint AS effective_qty
FROM cost_layers WHERE (sku_id, location_id) IN (...)
```

At sku=1 with N existing layers and M cost_depletions rows, this is O(N × log M) at minimum on indexed lookup, worst-case O(N²) on a hot pool.

Replace with: add column `cost_layers.effective_qty BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` (or actually equal to qty on insert). At Step 5c when writing cost_depletions, also UPDATE cost_layers SET effective_qty -= depleted_qty WHERE layer_id IN (...). Then Step 3 hydration becomes a plain index scan with no subquery.

Cost: small write amplification at depletion time (one extra UPDATE on the layer row, but cost_depletions rows are tiny and the UPDATE is per-row). Win: hydration becomes linear in touched layers, not quadratic in pool history.

### C. AVG / STD: hydration is already cheap (1 row per pool)
No meaningful win. Could go lazy (hydrate on first apply_one) but the eager bulk SELECT is one round-trip — saving it doesn't move the needle.

### D. Step 2.5 dedup-by-cost_depletions: skip when no FIFO depletions in SB
The dedup query reads cost_depletions for issue_id matching. For receipt-only batches or all-non-FIFO batches, this scan is empty by construction. Worth gating on (events contain FIFO depletion).

### E. Step 2.4 sku_method_assignments hydration: cache or pass in payload
`SELECT sku_id, method_id FROM poc_v21_sku_method_assignments WHERE sku_id = ANY($1)` runs per SB. The assignment is essentially static config. Could:
- Cache in shmem (invalidated on assignment change via NOTIFY or version bump)
- Or include method_id in the staging entry payload (caller passes it; router doesn't need it; committer reads from payload not the table)

Trades a table lookup for stale-cache risk on assignment changes. Worth measuring before committing.

### F. STD + wo_complete output qty>0: skip standard_costs lookup
The dispatch path already uses event.unit_cost directly. The Step 3 hydration loaded the row anyway. For SBs that contain ONLY wo_complete-output events on STD SKUs (rare; usually mixed with components which DO need std), skip. Low impact.

### G. qty==0 audit-only inv_adjust: no hydration needed at all
If a whole SB is qty==0 audit events, skip everything except Step 5a (posting_lines INSERT) and Step 12 (status UPSERT). Pathological-case win.

## Acceptance and follow-up

- This issue is the audit document. Carry forward the matrix when adding new event_kinds or cost_methods.
- File sub-issues for each shortcut that warrants implementation:
  - acct-00na — Shortcut A (FIFO eager hydration) — ALREADY FILED
  - Shortcut B (denormalized effective_qty) — file as separate bd issue
  - Shortcut D (dedup query gating) — file as separate bd issue
  - Shortcut E (method assignment caching) — file as separate bd issue, lower priority
  - Shortcuts C, F, G — note here but don't file unless measurement justifies

## Note on transactions vs cost methods

Calling out the broader split: BATCHING in the v2.1 architecture lives in two places.

1. **Cost-method-level batching**: Step 5 bulk UNNEST INSERT into cost_layers / cost_depletions / posting_lines etc. ALREADY BATCHED. One INSERT per table per SuperBatch. Good.

2. **Transaction-level overhead**: Step 2 (lex-locks), Step 3 (hydration), Step 4 (in-memory dispatch), Step 12 (status UPSERT) all run ONCE per SuperBatch regardless of envelope count. These are correctly amortized.

The bugs are NOT in the batching design. They're in Step 3 being eager when it could be demand-driven (Shortcut A), and in the hydration SQL being O(N²) when it could be O(N) (Shortcut B). Both are fixable without changing the architecture.

## Bench evidence

acct-cyu6 100k PO receipts, sku=1, batch_size_max=5000:
- FIFO (default): drain rate 746 evps, pipeline_ns/drain 928 ms, hydration accounted for >90% of pipeline time
- STD (correctly assigned): drain rate 181,402 evps, pipeline_ns/drain 8.3 ms

243× difference is almost entirely Step 3.

title: committer Step 3: demand-driven snapshot hydration — skip when SuperBatch has no state-reading events
description:
The committer's Step 3 (snapshot hydration in process_superbatch) eagerly loads pool state for EVERY (sku, location) touched in the SuperBatch, regardless of whether any event in the SB actually reads that state. For FIFO this means re-loading every existing `cost_layers` row + computing `effective_qty` via a correlated subquery on `cost_depletions` PER LAYER.

For receipt-only batches (po_receipt, inv_adjust with qty>0) this is 100% wasted work. Receipts just append a new layer; they do not depend on existing layers. AVG receipt updates the running average from prior state — needs hydration; but FIFO receipts don't.

## Smoking gun from acct-cyu6 bench

100k PO receipts at sku=1, distribution=single:

* FIFO (default before fix): pipeline_ns_per_drain = 928 ms at SB=32 → 29 ms/envelope; drain rate 746 evps.
* STD (after assigning method='std'): pipeline_ns_per_drain = 8.3 ms at SB=84 → 98 µs/envelope; drain rate 181,402 evps.

Same workload shape, same SuperBatch packing, same posting_lines / cost_layers writes. The 243× drain-rate difference is almost entirely Step 3: STD's `hydrate_standard_costs` is one row per (sku, loc); FIFO's `hydrate_fifo_layers` is:

```sql
SELECT layer_id, ..., 
  (qty - COALESCE((SELECT SUM(qty) FROM poc_v21_cost_depletions d 
                    WHERE d.layer_id = poc_v21_cost_layers.layer_id), 0)) AS effective_qty
  FROM poc_v21_cost_layers
 WHERE (sku_id, location_id) IN (...)
```

At sku=1 with N existing layers, this runs N rows with a correlated subquery per row → O(N²) per drain, growing as the run progresses.

## The fix

Step 3 should inspect the events in the SuperBatch and skip hydration when no event in this SB depletes inventory from the touched pool. Concretely:

```rust
let needs_fifo_hydration: HashSet<(i64, i64)> = events.iter()
    .filter(|e| event_depletes_pool(e))  // wo_complete component, so_shipment, scrap, op_move source, ...
    .map(|e| (e.sku_id, e.location_id))
    .collect();

let fifo_pools_to_hydrate = fifo_pools.iter()
    .filter(|k| needs_fifo_hydration.contains(k))
    .copied().collect();

if !fifo_pools_to_hydrate.is_empty() {
    hydrate_fifo_layers(...);
}
```

Same shape for AVG (depletions need running avg; pure receipts don't — receipts re-roll the avg via roll_in which only reads its own pool's current state, so we still need to hydrate to roll the average forward; this needs careful design).

For STD this is already a no-op (one row per pool); leave as-is.

## Secondary problem visible in same bench

The hydration SQL itself uses a correlated subquery per layer to compute `effective_qty`. Even when hydration IS needed, this O(N²) shape is expensive. Alternatives:

* Maintain `effective_qty` on the `cost_layers` row, decremented at depletion time (denormalized but fast)
* Move depletions into a per-(sku, loc) materialized view that's incrementally maintained
* Rewrite the correlated subquery as a single LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY (linear pass over depletions, not per-layer scan)

These are separate optimizations; the primary fix is "don't hydrate when not needed."

## Scope

Touches `process_superbatch` in `committer.rs` and the per-method hydration helpers. Must preserve correctness:
- Snapshot rollback on per-envelope failure expects the snapshot to be populated for touched pools. If we skip hydration but a depletion event later fires (impossible by construction if we only skip when no depletion exists in the SB), would crash. Easy to assert.
- AVG roll_in on receipts: re-reads pool.avg_unit_cost from snapshot. If we skip hydration on a receipt-only AVG batch, snapshot is empty → roll_in starts from zero. WRONG. AVG needs hydration on receipts too (running average rolling).

So this is FIFO-specific: skip Step 3 FIFO hydration when SB has no FIFO depletions. AVG must still hydrate. STD is already lazy.

## Acceptance

- New event-type classifier `event_depletes_pool(event)` returning bool
- Step 3 skips `hydrate_fifo_layers` when no event in the SB depletes any of the touched FIFO pools
- Regression: 100k PO receipts at sku=1 with method=FIFO should hit a drain rate within 2× of the STD-method result (currently 243× slower; should be at most 2× because real FIFO writes do MORE work than STD due to per-receipt layer insert, but not 243× more)
- Existing FIFO tests with depletion-bearing SBs continue to pass
- acct-cyu6 bench re-runnable as a measurement gate; FIFO single-distribution drain rate ≥ 50k evps after fix
acceptance_criteria:
- `event_depletes_pool(event: &PocV21Event) -> bool` helper added
- Step 3 in process_superbatch builds the set of pools that need hydration based on events-that-deplete and intersects with touched pools per method
- FIFO-method receipts on a receipt-only SB skip hydration; envelope success rate unchanged
- Bench re-run: po-single-N100000 with method=FIFO drain rate ≥ 50,000 evps (currently 746)
- All existing committer tests pass (no correctness regression)

title: push 100k PO receipts at current settings, two SKU distributions, persisted payload
description:
Simple ceiling probe. No deps. Current GUCs as-is (batch_size_max=50, router_window_size=1000, batch_window_us=500 — note batch_window_us is dead code, that's fine for this probe; see acct-0sc4 separately if a follow-up).

Goal: push 100k po_receipt envelopes through the v2.1 PoC as fast as possible, with payloads persisted to disk, on two SKU distributions. See what the system actually does.

## Two distributions

- `single`: every envelope hits (sku=1, location=1). Maximum pool-key overlap. The router's affinity grouping has to deal with 100k envelopes targeting one node. If it packs, avg_envelopes_per_sb should approach batch_size_max=50. If it doesn't pack here, it never will.
- `uniform_1000`: sku = (iter % 1000) + 1, location=1. ~100 envelopes per SKU pool. Router's affinity grouping has lower per-pool collision rate; we measure what the architecture does in the "real-world" no-deliberate-hot-spot case.

## Persistence

JSONL one envelope per line:
  bench/payloads/po-{distribution}-N100000.jsonl

Each line:
  {"correlation_id":"<uuid>","event_type":"po_receipt",
   "payload":{"sku_id":<i64>,"location_id":1,"qty":1,"unit_cost":100,
              "issue_id":<iter>,"business_date_jdate":20221,
              "doc_chrono":<iter>,"document_id":9000000+<iter>},
   "pool_keys":{"sku":[[<sku>,1]],"wip":[]}}

correlation_id deterministic via UUIDv5 over namespace + "po-{distribution}-N100000:{iter}". Re-running the generator produces byte-identical file. sha256 the file and write a sidecar .meta.json with the hash + generator commit + envelope count.

## Submission shape

Fire-and-forget. Read JSONL into memory once. Spawn N tokio backends (start N=8, match nproc). Each pulls envelopes round-robin via shared Arc<Mutex<Iter>> or atomic counter. Submit via single sqlx connection per backend. NO per-envelope polling.

After all enqueues return: bulk-poll submission_status:
  SELECT correlation_id, processed_at, state FROM poc_v21_submission_status
   WHERE correlation_id = ANY($1::uuid[])
every 1s until COUNT = 100000 or 60s elapsed since last enqueue returned. (Architecture should drain 100k in well under that on a single-shape PO workload; if not, that's the finding.)

## Measurements

Three throughput numbers, all reported separately:
- submission_rate = 100000 / (last_enqueue_returned - first_enqueue_returned)
- commit_rate    = 100000 / (max(processed_at) - min(processed_at))
- end_to_end     = 100000 / (max(processed_at) - first_enqueue_returned)

Per-envelope latency (e2e) = processed_at - enqueue_returned_at, derived from the bulk poll. Histogram via hdrhistogram.

Counter snapshots (before-all-enqueues vs after-drain-complete):
- Router: superbatch_count, total_envelopes, max_envelope_count, envelope_histogram, ticks_total, cross_sb_for_update_waits, force_pack_count
- Committer: drains_total, pipeline_ns_total, pipeline_count, tx_failures, takeover_count, eject_count, backpressure_count

## Output

bench/results-m8-ceiling/po-{distribution}-N100000.json with all three throughputs, latency histogram quantiles, counter deltas, envelope outcome counts (committed/failed/missing).

## What we expect to learn

- Whether the system is ingress-bound or commit-bound (compare submission_rate vs commit_rate)
- Whether the router actually packs at sku=1 (avg_envelopes_per_sb at distribution=single)
- Real-world distribution effect (single vs uniform_1000)

## Out of scope

- 5-replication / IQR (M8.2 territory; this is a single probe to see the ceiling)
- GUC sweep (current settings only)
- Other event kinds (PO receipt only)
- Other cost methods (standard cost only)
- N-sweep (single N; we don't have batch ingress so per-call cost will set the ceiling regardless)
acceptance_criteria:
- bench/payloads/po-single-N100000.jsonl + sha256 sidecar exists, byte-stable across reruns of generator
- bench/payloads/po-uniform_1000-N100000.jsonl + sha256 sidecar exists, byte-stable across reruns of generator
- Replay runner reads JSONL, submits open-loop, bulk-polls terminal state
- Result JSON files written for both distributions
- 100k envelopes either reach terminal state OR runner reports the missing count (does not panic)
- Result file reports submission_rate, commit_rate, end_to_end_rate, latency p50/p99/p999, router + committer counter deltas, top wait_event
close_reason: Ceiling probe complete. Drain rate 181k evps on hot pool; e2e 1944 evps submission-bound. Exposed architectural shortcuts now filed as acct-hg9g (audit) + acct-00na/3ypi/h6ha (per-shortcut sub-issues).

title: wire batch_window_us into router_tick(): time-coalesce emission gate
description:
The GUC `poc_v21.batch_window_us` is registered (lib.rs:791-799), reader function `batch_window_us_now()` exists (lib.rs:514), default = 500µs (from `GucSetting::<i32>::new(500)`). But `batch_window_us_now()` is never called — confirmed by compile warning:

  warning: function `batch_window_us_now` is never used
     --> src/lib.rs:514:15

So the knob is dead code. `router_tick()` runs every 50ms (BGWorker latch wait) and emits whatever is pending at the moment; there is no time-coalesce mechanism.

This is the load-bearing knob for the queue-time-vs-batch-size tradeoff. Without it, the architecture's "wait briefly to fill a SuperBatch" claim is unmeasurable. acct-lm20 (M8.x ceiling bench) cannot do its GUC sweep without this.

## What "wired" means

`router_tick()` should respect `batch_window_us` by holding emission for envelopes that have been pending for LESS than `batch_window_us`. Concretely:

1. Each StagingEntry already records `enqueued_at_ns` (verify in code; if not, add it — needed for fairness backstop already)
2. In `collect_candidates()` or in a new gating step, compute `now_ns - candidate.enqueued_at_ns` for the OLDEST candidate
3. If `now - oldest_enqueued > batch_window_us * 1000`: emit normally (current behavior)
4. If `now - oldest_enqueued <= batch_window_us * 1000`: defer emission — return 0 from this tick, let the next 50ms tick (or earlier wake-up via enqueue signal) re-evaluate

This is conservative: we still emit if even ONE envelope has waited longer than the window. The window is "max queue wait", not "minimum queue wait" — we don't artificially hold an envelope that's been pending long enough.

Implementation note: BGWorker tick interval (50ms) is much coarser than typical batch_window_us values (50µs..50000µs default range). For batch_window_us < tick interval, the effective window is dominated by the tick interval — that's a real constraint of the BGWorker design, not a wiring bug. Document it.

Alternative implementation: instead of gating in `router_tick`, change the BGWorker's `wait_latch` duration to `min(batch_window_us, current_50ms)` so it wakes up earlier when small windows are configured. More invasive; defer to follow-up if measurements show the 50ms floor is the actual bottleneck.

## What we measure post-wiring

With the wiring in place, acct-lm20's GUC sweep includes batch_window_us ∈ {0, 100, 500, 5000, 50000} on both `single` and `uniform_1000` distributions. Expected behavior:

- batch_window_us=0: today's behavior (no wait)
- batch_window_us=500: small wait, modest packing increase
- batch_window_us=5000 (5ms): noticeable wait, more packing
- batch_window_us=50000 (50ms): one full tick of wait, maximum packing under the BGWorker constraint

The curve directly measures the queue-time-vs-batch-size tradeoff the user asked about.
acceptance_criteria:
- `batch_window_us_now()` is called from `router_tick()` (no more dead-code warning)
- When the oldest pending candidate has `now_ns - enqueued_at_ns <= batch_window_us * 1000`, `router_tick()` returns 0 (no emission) for THIS tick
- When the oldest pending candidate has waited longer, normal emission proceeds (current behavior)
- StagingEntry.enqueued_at_ns is populated at `poc_v21_enqueue` time (verify existing or add)
- Existing tests still pass (no regression; default batch_window_us=500µs is small enough that the 50ms tick interval dominates in most current bench shapes)
- Integration test: with batch_window_us=10000 (10ms), a single envelope enqueued at t=0 does NOT emit at the next tick fired at t=2ms; it emits at the tick fired at t≥10ms (verifies the gate fires)
- Integration test: with batch_window_us=0, behavior is identical to current — every tick that finds pending candidates emits (no regression)
close_reason:
Shipped as 449a61b. router_tick now consults poc_v21.batch_window_us as a time-coalesce gate: if oldest candidate age < window, tick defers (returns 0) and increments router_window_defers_total. CandidateMeta carries enqueued_at_micros from StagingEntry (no schema change). GUC range widened to 0..5_000_000 (was 50..50_000) — 0 disables, default 500us stays conservative (dominated by 50ms BGWorker tick).

Tests/acceptance_v21_batch_window.rs covers both directions:
- window=0: emits immediately, defers_total stays 0
- window=2_000_000us: immediate tick defers, post-sleep tick emits

Bench at optimal cell (count=100k, spread=100, normal, ib=5, rsb=5000, N=8, drain_batch=2, K=5+warm):

  GUC                e2e_median  CV%   avgSB
  500us (default)         7071  1.1%   7.0
  50000us (50ms)          7791  1.4%   7.3    +10.2% vs default

50ms gate yields slightly bigger SBs (avgSB 7.0→7.3) AND a more rhythmic BGWorker cycle (deferred ticks are cheap early returns) — net +10% e2e and +12% submit_evps. The default stays conservative; production tuning to 50000us is documented here as the measured optimum for steady-state STD receipt workloads. Acceptance criteria (window respected by router_tick, observability counter present, tests for both window=0 and window>0 cases) met.

v21 acceptance suite: 33 green / 0 red.

title: M8.x-ceiling: PO-receipt-only fire-and-forget bench with persisted payload + SKU-distribution baseline
description:
M8.2 measured submit-and-poll closed-loop throughput on the S2 wo_complete shape and topped out at 385 evps — but that's a measurement of the BENCH, not the architecture. To find the architecture's actual throughput ceiling we need:

1. The simplest possible payload (PO receipt at standard cost)
2. Open-loop submission ("submit as fast as possible", no per-envelope poll)
3. Persisted payloads (JSONL on disk) so runs are bit-identical replays
4. Two SKU-distribution baselines that bracket affinity packing:
   - SKU=1 across all envelopes → max overlap → router should pack toward batch_size_max
   - SKU uniform over 1..1000 → zero deterministic overlap → singletons unless batch_window_us coalesces

Then, with the ceiling established, sweep router GUCs to characterize queue-wait-time vs batch-size tradeoff under each distribution.

PO receipt rationale:
- Single-method (standard cost is simplest)
- Single event_kind
- 2 posting_lines per envelope (raw debit + ap_unsettled credit) — minimum ledger work
- No WIP, no components, no co-products
- pool_keys = [(sku, location)] — single pool node per envelope

Standard cost rationale (vs FIFO):
- No layer rows to seed/maintain
- No depletion-time decisions
- Pure dispatcher cost — the architecture's "common case"
design:
## Architecture

Three-phase pipeline:

**Phase 1 — Generator (offline, one-time per payload variant)**

`tests/common/m8_ceiling_generator.rs` produces a deterministic JSONL file:

  {"correlation_id":"<uuid>","event_type":"po_receipt","payload":{...},"pool_keys":{...}}
  ...one per line, N lines total

Per (distribution, count) tuple. SKU distributions:
- `single`: every envelope targets (sku=1, location=1)
- `uniform_1000`: sku = (iter % 1000) + 1, location=1

Each envelope's payload:
  {"sku_id": <i64>, "location_id": 1, "qty": 1, "unit_cost": 100,
   "issue_id": <iter>, "business_date_jdate": 20221,
   "doc_chrono": <iter>, "document_id": 9_000_000 + <iter>}

Files written to: `poc/queue-extension-v21/bench/payloads/po-{distribution}-N{count}.jsonl`
+ sidecar `po-{distribution}-N{count}.meta.json` with:
  - generator version (commit sha at generation time)
  - rng seed
  - sha256 of the JSONL file
  - envelope count + distribution descriptor

Determinism: correlation_id derived from `UUIDv5(namespace, "<distribution>:<iter>")` (NOT UUIDv4) so re-generating the same (distribution, count) yields byte-identical files. Replay against the same file produces the same workload.

Counts to generate first: 1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000 envelopes per distribution. 100k is the primary "ceiling" target; 1M is the soak run.

**Phase 2 — Replay runner**

`tests/bench_m8_ceiling.rs` reads the JSONL, fires `poc_v21_enqueue` calls open-loop. Two designs to evaluate:

  Design A — N tokio tasks, each pulls envelopes round-robin from the JSONL until exhausted. Each task submits via single sqlx connection. NO per-envelope poll. Measures submission rate first, then waits for ALL correlation_ids to reach terminal state via a single bulk poll (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM submission_status WHERE correlation_id = ANY($1)` every 100ms until count = N).

  Design B — preload all envelopes into one in-memory Vec, then N async tasks pull-with-Mutex<Arc<Vec>>. Same submission shape; cheaper iteration since no JSONL reparse during submission window.

Pick (B) — JSONL parse is offline-phase cost; we want to isolate the system's submission cost during the bench window.

**Latency sampling**

Per-envelope latency = (enqueue_call_returned_at - submission_status.committed_at). We DO NOT poll each correlation_id individually — that's the closed-loop trap. Instead:

- Capture `enqueue_call_returned_at` per envelope in a Vec<(Uuid, Instant)>
- After all enqueues complete (or hit a soft timeout), bulk-SELECT submission_status for all correlation_ids: `SELECT correlation_id, processed_at, state FROM submission_status WHERE correlation_id = ANY($1::uuid[])`
- Per envelope: latency = (processed_at - enqueue_call_returned_at). If row not found / state not committed → failure.

Tradeoff: this measures **terminal-state-after-the-fact**, NOT live latency. We get the right histogram but not real-time observability. For the ceiling measurement that's the right tradeoff — we want max throughput, and live polling at 1ms per backend would dominate the workload.

**Phase 3 — Throughput measurement**

Submission throughput = N / (last_enqueue_returned - first_enqueue_returned)
Commit throughput   = N / (max(processed_at) - min(processed_at))  -- "wall time the system took to drain"
End-to-end          = N / (max(processed_at) - first_enqueue_returned)

All three matter. End-to-end is the user-facing number; commit-throughput tells us if the system is committer-bound or ingress-bound.

## SKU distribution sweep — two cells per count

| cell | distribution | overlap | expected SB shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| `single`       | sku=1 every envelope     | 100% pool-key collision | every pending envelope joins one affinity component; router emits ⌈N/batch_size_max⌉ SBs each at batch_size_max |
| `uniform_1000` | sku uniform over [1..1000] | ~N/1000 collision rate at low N; rises with N | mostly singletons at low N; affinity packing emerges as load increases |

For `single`: the router's affinity packing MUST work. If it doesn't pack at this distribution, the design is broken at its core claim. This is the strongest signal we can produce.

For `uniform_1000`: shows the "real-world" case where envelopes mostly don't overlap. Quantifies what the architecture costs when affinity packing doesn't help.

## GUC sweep (phase 4, after baselines)

Once the two baseline runs establish the ceiling, sweep:
- batch_size_max ∈ {1, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000} — at sku=1 distribution, batch_size_max directly bounds SB size, so we measure fsync amortization curve
- router_window_size ∈ {100, 1000, 10000} — how much pending state the router consumes per tick
- (deferred until wired) batch_window_us ∈ {0 = current, 100, 500, 5000} — time-coalesce knob

Per (cell, GUC) combination: 1 bench run (no 5-replication yet — that's M8.2 territory and we're trying to find the curve, not pin medians). If a setting looks interesting, do 5-replication on just that point.

## Outputs

Per run, write `bench/results-m8-ceiling/{distribution}_N{count}_bsm{batch_size_max}_rws{router_window_size}.json`:

  {
    "payload": "po-single-N100000.jsonl",
    "payload_sha256": "...",
    "n_envelopes": 100000,
    "distribution": "single",
    "gucs": {"batch_size_max": 50, "router_window_size": 1000, "batch_window_us": 500},
    "submission": { "wall_ms": ..., "rate_evps": ..., "first_enqueue_at_ns": ..., "last_enqueue_at_ns": ... },
    "commit": { "wall_ms": ..., "rate_evps": ..., "first_processed_at": ..., "last_processed_at": ... },
    "end_to_end": { "wall_ms": ..., "rate_evps": ... },
    "latency_e2e_us": { "p50": ..., "p99": ..., "p999": ..., "max": ... },
    "router": { "superbatch_count": ..., "avg_envelopes_per_sb": ..., "max_envelope_count": ..., "envelope_histogram": [...] },
    "committer": { "drains_total": ..., "pipeline_ns_total": ..., "pipeline_count": ..., "tx_failures": ... },
    "envelope_outcomes": { "committed": ..., "failed": ..., "missing": ... },
    "wait_events_top5": [...]
  }
acceptance_criteria:
- Generator produces `bench/payloads/po-single-N{1000,10000,100000}.jsonl` + `po-uniform_1000-N{1000,10000,100000}.jsonl` with sidecar metadata
- Payload files content-stable: re-running generator with same (distribution, count, seed) produces byte-identical output (verify by sha256)
- Replay runner reads JSONL, submits open-loop via N tokio backends, captures per-envelope enqueue-return timestamps in memory, bulk-polls submission_status post-submission
- All N envelopes either reach terminal state within bounded wall-time OR runner reports the failed/missing count without panicking
- Throughput numbers (submission, commit, end-to-end) all reported separately
- Latency histogram derived from (processed_at − enqueue_returned_at) per envelope
- Router + committer counter deltas captured per run
- At sku=1 distribution: `avg_envelopes_per_sb` ≥ 10 at N=100000 with batch_size_max=50 (the affinity-packing claim is actually exercised — if this acceptance fails, the affinity router has a bug)
- Two-cell baseline output written before any GUC sweep begins
- GUC sweep cells named consistently so M9.1 can ingest

Stretch (file as follow-up if effort emerges): batch_window_us wired into `router_tick()` so the time-coalesce knob actually does something.
notes:
Update 2026-05-19: filed acct-0sc4 to wire batch_window_us (currently dead code). lm20 now depends on 0sc4.

Sweep axes for the queue-time-vs-batch-size measurement:
- batch_window_us ∈ {0, 100, 500, 5000, 50000}  -- queue-time knob (acct-0sc4)
- batch_size_max ∈ {1, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000}  -- batch-size knob
- router_window_size ∈ {1000, 10000}  -- scan window (secondary; doesn't bound emission)

Cross product is 5×6×2 = 60 cells per distribution; 120 across both distributions. Run as a single-replication scan first to find interesting regions, then 5x replicate the corners.

Removed prior "(deferred until wired)" defer — wiring is the prerequisite, not a stretch.

title: batch-enqueue API: poc_v21_enqueue_batch(envelopes JSONB) for true batch ingress
description:
The v2.1 PoC's `poc_v21_enqueue` accepts exactly one envelope per call. To submit 1000 PO receipts the application must make 1000 separate `SELECT poc_v21_enqueue(...)` calls — 1000 submission_status INSERTs, 1000 LWLock acquires on the staging queue, 1000 arena allocations.

The architecture's "batch N envelopes per commit" claim lives entirely on the router→committer side; ingress is per-envelope. This is a gap for batch-shaped producers — month-end close, daily warehouse uploads, bulk invoice runs, EDI inbound feeds — which are at least as common as stream-shaped in ERP workloads.

Spec coverage: poc-v2.1.md line 1796 ("Single-SKU workloads should produce SuperBatches at exactly batch_size_max except for the tail") assumes batching emerges from concurrent overlapping per-call enqueues, not from a batch ingress API. There is no spec text for batch ingress.

Proposed API:

  poc_v21_enqueue_batch(envelopes JSONB) RETURNS BIGINT

Where `envelopes` is a JSON array of objects matching the existing single-envelope shape:
  [
    {"correlation_id": "uuid", "event_type": "po_receipt",
     "payload": {...}, "pool_keys": {"sku":[...], "wip":[...]}},
    ...
  ]

Returns the count of envelopes enqueued.

Implementation outline (one-pass over the array):
1. Parse + validate every envelope (fail-fast: if envelope N is malformed, abort the whole call; no partial enqueue)
2. Bulk-INSERT N rows into submission_status in ONE statement (one WAL record group amortizes N row writes)
3. Allocate ONE arena block sized to fit all payload + pool_keys bytes (one LWLock on SPILLOVER_ARENA, not N)
4. Reserve N consecutive staging-queue slots via a single fetch_add(N) on STAGING_QUEUE.tail, then write StagingEntry data into each (no per-slot LWLock churn — the existing tail-advance is already lock-free; the LWLock is for the slot-state CAS, which still happens per-slot but at least the queue head pointer advances atomically)
5. ONE backpressure check on `tail + N ≤ head + capacity` before reserving; CV-wait once on full instead of N times

The router/committer downstream is unchanged — StagingEntries are still consumed one at a time, but now they arrive in continuous runs that the router will scan in one tick (with router_window_size=1000, batch_size_max=50, a 1000-envelope ingress lands fully in the next router tick).

Out of scope:
- Mixed-event_type within one batch is allowed (the per-envelope event_type stays per-envelope)
- durable_queue flag is per-batch (all or none) — adding a per-envelope flag inflates the JSON; defer if needed
- Idempotency: correlation_ids must be distinct across the batch (callers responsibility; staging-side dedup is per-correlation_id already)

This also unlocks the M8.2 → M8.3 → M9.1 bench gap: today's submit-and-poll bench caps offered load at N × (1/latency) because each backend holds 1 outstanding envelope. With batch ingress a single backend can push 1000 envelopes/call, letting the staging queue actually fill up and the router actually pack. The "10k-100k evps" target the architecture promises cannot be measured under the current API.
design:
Decisions to lock before implementing:

1. **One-shot fail-or-succeed**: if any envelope in the array is invalid, the whole call fails (no partial enqueue). Reason: caller can't recover from "we enqueued envelopes 0..473, but 474 was malformed" without knowing which 474 made it; better to fail atomically. Down side: a single bad row in a 1000-batch poisons the whole batch.

2. **JSONB array vs UNNEST**: spec the parameter as JSONB array. Alternatives considered:
   - `UNNEST(correlation_ids[], event_types[], payloads[], pool_keys[])`: forces 4 parallel arrays, fragile if lengths differ. Rejected.
   - Anonymous record type: pgrx representation is awkward. Rejected.
   - JSONB is the closest match to today's single-envelope shape (3 JSONB args become 1 JSONB array of {3 keys}).

3. **submission_status bulk INSERT shape**: `INSERT INTO submission_status (correlation_id, ...) SELECT ... FROM UNNEST($1::uuid[], $2::text[], ...) AS t(c, e, ...) ON CONFLICT (correlation_id) DO NOTHING`. Mirrors the existing single-INSERT path; preserves the idempotency semantics on correlation_id re-submission.

4. **Status row INSERT mode**: respect the GUC `poc_v21.status_insert_mode` per-batch. caller_intx mode bulk-INSERTs all rows inside the caller's user-tx; committer_lazy skips entirely (committer creates rows at terminal-state determination). Mixed-mode within a batch is not allowed (GUC is cluster-wide).

5. **Arena allocation strategy**: single large block sized to fit `Σ (payload_bytes + pool_keys_bytes)`. Each StagingEntry's offset points into the contiguous block. On failure (arena_full), the WHOLE batch rolls back — no partial arena writes; reserve-then-commit on the arena block index. Existing arena code is lock-held-then-released; this needs a "reserve N bytes, return offset, write later" extension.

6. **Backpressure**: one CV-wait on `tail + N > head + capacity`. If batch_size > staging_queue_capacity (POC_V21_STAGING_QUEUE_SIZE), raise an error — caller fragmented their own batch wrong. (Today's queue size is small enough that this matters: at 2048 slots a batch of 4096 envelopes can't fit even if the queue is empty.)

7. **per-call latency cost vs per-call benefit**: bulk path's fixed overhead (parse JSONB array, allocate larger arena block, build the UNNEST arrays for status INSERT) should beat N × single-call cost for N >= ~10. For N=1 the bulk path is strictly worse; callers that submit one envelope at a time should keep using `poc_v21_enqueue`. We do not deprecate the single-call API.

8. **JSONB validation**: the single-call path validates payload + pool_keys via parse_pool_keys() + payload serialization. Batch path runs the same validations per element; fail-fast on first error with index in the error message ("envelope[473]: pool_keys missing 'sku' key").

9. **Replay flag**: durable_queue is a per-batch boolean. All envelopes in one batch share the flag. The PoC has no client requirement for mixed durable/transient envelopes; if that emerges, add a per-envelope `durable_queue` to the JSON object.

Open questions:
- Should the function return the array of correlation_ids in order of enqueue, or just the count? (Caller already knows the correlation_ids since they generated them; returning them is redundant. Count is enough. Defer to implementation.)
- Should we expose a Rust-side `enqueue_many` helper that the test runner can use for bench purposes, separate from the SQL surface? (Yes — once SQL works, the bench runner builds the JSON array client-side and calls the SQL fn; a Rust-side helper is duplication.)
acceptance_criteria:
- `poc_v21_enqueue_batch(envelopes JSONB)` registered as pg_extern, returns BIGINT count
- Single-statement bulk INSERT into submission_status for all N envelopes (verified by EXPLAIN/log)
- Single SPILLOVER_ARENA LWLock acquire for the whole batch (verified by counting `arena_reserve` calls in instrumentation)
- Single STAGING_QUEUE.tail.fetch_add(N) for the whole batch
- One CV-wait on backpressure if the staging queue cannot accommodate N envelopes
- Atomic failure: malformed envelope at index k aborts the whole call; no rows in submission_status, no arena writes, no staging entries created
- Backwards-compatible: existing `poc_v21_enqueue` single-envelope path unchanged; both APIs coexist
- Integration test: enqueue a batch of 1000 wo_complete envelopes; assert all 1000 reach terminal state (committed) within a 30s window
- Bench addendum: M8.2 statistical runner gains a batch-ingress mode (POC_M82_BATCH_SIZE env var); produces S2 N-sweep results under batch ingress for direct comparison with per-call results
notes:
Sweep complete (commit 70240f9). Stage-timing instrumented (separate commit pending). Max e2e = 4533 evps at (spread=100, normal, ingress=5, rsb=5000, N=8, committer_lazy).

Stage breakdown at e2e=4225 measurement (avg per SuperBatch, avgSB=7.9 envelopes):
- parse:        434 µs (12.9%)
- pre_apply:   1297 µs (38.6%)  — locks + caller_tx + dedup + hydrate
- apply:         22 µs ( 0.7%)  — Rust apply_one
- bulk_insert: 1529 µs (45.5%)  — 6 conditional INSERTs (3 fire for std)
- post:         506 µs (15.0%)  — Step 12 status UPSERTs + Step 14 cleanup
- TOTAL:       3362 µs/SB       = ~425 µs/envelope

Bottleneck is SQL writes (Steps 2 + 5 + 12 = 99% of pipeline). Rust apply is essentially free.

Architectural follow-ups filed (separate issues):

Bulk_insert (45.5%) optimization paths:
- acct-xwu3 P2: skip cost_layers INSERT for std (dead-weight rows; ~10-15% e2e lift)
- acct-gfvb P2: CTE-merge active INSERTs into one SPI call (blocked-by acct-xwu3)
- acct-y1ci P3: drop posting_lines RETURNING (blocked-by acct-xwu3)
- acct-meov P2: heap_multi_insert via FFI — bypass executor (blocked-by xwu3+gfvb; ~30-40% e2e lift)
- acct-83oq P2: COPY FROM via in-memory tuple stream (alternative to meov; blocked-by xwu3+gfvb)
- acct-6kcx P2: batch N SBs per drain transaction (orthogonal; ~10-15% e2e lift)

Pre_apply (38.6%) optimization paths:
- acct-a2sj P2: cache pool_locks INSERT — skip when row already exists (~2-3% e2e lift)
- acct-ed7u P2: cache standard_costs / avg_pool_state hydration (~3-5% e2e lift)

Estimated stacked-win upper bound: acct-xwu3 + acct-meov + acct-6kcx + acct-a2sj + acct-ed7u → ~8000-10000 e2e evps (still 5-10× below v2 shmem rollup's 67k, but a meaningful 2× lift). The v2 architecture's 67k requires structural shmem-rollup state — separate from this issue tree.
close_reason: Shipped batch API + acceptance tests + full sweep harness + measurements (max 4533 e2e at ib=5 N=8 committer_lazy spread=100 normal). Architectural ceiling identified; drain-side optimizations are separate follow-up scope.

title: committer-memory-ordering-policy-doc (Q9+Q8+B7+L3)
description:
Doc-only consolidation across 4 audit findings:

Q9: Atomic ordering mix (Relaxed / Acquire / Release) used inconsistently across committer.rs without a documented policy. Future maintainers (or future me) can't tell whether a Relaxed read is correct or an oversight.

Q8: Histogram uses Relaxed — correct as-is; cover under same policy block.

B7: Step 14 CAS-2→0 fallback race window. Reviewer correct the window exists; the in-line comment justifies it (M5b.2 / acct-kt61). Expand the inline comment with the explicit invariant: eject_count incremented BEFORE valid 3→1, with Release ordering, so observed_eject==0 + valid==2 ⇒ no eject in flight. Reference the dead-PID rescue path that handles the slot if the race does happen.

L3: ordinal_to_pl_id mechanism (line 1196 region) — necessary indirection for RETURNING-then-FK-resolution. Add 5-line doc comment explaining: positions are stable across the cost_layers insert because we INSERT ... RETURNING id ORDER BY ... and zip with the original ordering.

Fix: add a 30-line policy block at the top of committer.rs documenting:
(a) valid state transitions use Release on advance + Acquire on observe
(b) committer_pid ownership claim uses Acquire on claim, Relaxed on release-after-failure (no other thread depends on the release timing)
(c) stats counters use Relaxed (monotonic, monitoring-only)
