title: Phase 1 Epic C: wac_retroactive implementation
description:
Retroactive Perpetual Weighted Average. Per Oracle/PeopleSoft: 'weighted avg calculated after each putaway just like perpetual, BUT recomputed at end of period and applied retroactively.' Hybrid of wac_perpetual (live chain mid-period) and wac_periodic (close-time correction).

DIFFERENCE FROM wac_periodic. Periodic uses ONE final period avg = Σ(in-period receipts value)/Σ(in-period qty), applied to all depletions in the period. Retroactive maintains the perpetual chain semantics — each depletion gets re-costed at THE RUNNING AVG IT SHOULD HAVE HAD given full-period data, including late-arriving receipts that were originally booked out of order.

USE CASE. Receipts physically arrived 2026-04-05 but the paperwork didn't post until 2026-04-15 (after the 2026-04-10 depletion). Mid-period: depletion on 2026-04-10 used running avg WITHOUT the 2026-04-05 receipt (which hadn't been posted yet). At close: the 2026-04-05 receipt is in the period (business_date < 2026-04-10), so the depletion's running avg should have included it. Variance corrects.

DEPENDS ON: closed acct-s6n (period-close machinery), closed acct-qfj (wac_periodic provisional-flagging infrastructure — reused), closed acct-1vr (per-class qty divisor). All foundations are in place.

LOCKED-IN DESIGN DECISIONS (acct-9tw memo, 2026-05-01, user confirmed):

D1 — CHRONOLOGICAL REPLAY ORDER. Walk pool events ordered by (business_date ASC, posted_at ASC, transfer.id ASC). business_date is primary; posted_at (TIMESTAMPTZ, microsecond resolution from clock_timestamp) breaks same-day ties; transfer.id is the final deterministic tiebreaker. Closest to ERP convention; fully deterministic.

D2 — IN-PERIOD EVENT SCOPE. The replay includes ALL events affecting the pool in this period, not just wac_retroactive-flagged ones. This means cross-period variance corrections, prior-period close-time corrections that have business_date in this period, and other workflows' postings to the pool all participate in the running chain. Most accurate model — replays the 'true' perpetual chain as it should have been.

D3 — WIP CLASS DEFERRED. Source pool of kind inv_value_wip raises P0006. Same restriction as wac_periodic — recursive cost-chain analysis across linked pools is out of scope for Phase 1. Tracked under acct-p7v (Phase 2 Epic J: wac_periodic + wac_retroactive across WIP pools).

D4 — VARIANCE ROUTING. Same 2-transfer pattern as wac_periodic, routed through variance_wac_retroactive (already seeded from s6n in USD + EUR). Both legs use reason='cost_restate'. Net effect: variance_wac_retroactive nets to zero per close, but provides audit visibility.

D5 — PRE-PERIOD POOL STATE. Initial running state at period start = SUM over transfers WHERE pool affected AND business_date < period_opens, signed by debit/credit. Reuses the per-class qty SUM pattern from migration 0030.

D6 — REPLAY ALGORITHM. PL/pgSQL FOR loop walking ordered events:
  - Initialize cumulative (pool_value, pool_qty) from pre-period state.
  - For each event in chronological order:
    * If receipt (debit to pool): pool_value += amount; pool_qty += qty.
    * If depletion (credit from pool): recomputed_avg = pool_value / pool_qty (truncating BIGINT); recomputed_amount = qty × recomputed_avg; pool_value -= recomputed_amount; pool_qty -= qty.
    * If the depletion is wac_retroactive-flagged in transfers_provisional: variance = recomputed_amount - original_provisional_amount; post 2-transfer batch routing through variance_wac_retroactive; mark finalized.
    * Other depletions (e.g., from prior periods' closes) update running state but don't post variance.

D7 — INTEGER ARITHMETIC. Truncating BIGINT division. Cumulative truncation effects across the replay are the same as they would have been if the perpetual chain had been built correctly mid-period. No interpolation/rounding correction — matches wac_perpetual semantics.

SUB-ISSUES:
- 9tw.1: Schema/dispatcher (compute_amount + post_inventory_adjustment + post_transfers flagging + close hook real body)
- 9tw.2: Test matrix (out-of-order arrivals, late receipts, multi-depletion replay, multi-pool, period boundaries)
- 9tw.3: Doc updates (§4.2 design doc, db/README, CLAUDE.md retire stub-hook bullet for wac_retroactive)

OUT OF SCOPE:
- WIP class (acct-p7v).
- wac_periodic + wac_retroactive on same SKU (cost_method is per-SKU).
- Sub-second timestamp resolution issues (clock_timestamp microsecond is enough).
- Concurrent close_period serialization (already handled by close_period FOR UPDATE on periods row).

ACCEPTANCE:
- Receive 100@5 on 2026-04-01, deplete 30 on 2026-04-10 (running avg=5, provisional=5).
- Late-booked receipt 100@9 with business_date 2026-04-05, posted on 2026-04-15.
- After close: depletion on 2026-04-10 had a recomputed running avg = (500+900)/(100+100) at that point... wait, no — only receipts with business_date <= 2026-04-10 count. The 2026-04-05 receipt qualifies (business_date 2026-04-05 < 2026-04-10). So recomputed_avg at depletion = 1400/200 = 7. Variance = 30 × (7-5) = 60.
- Variance posted via variance_wac_retroactive routing.

title: Phase 1 Epic B: wac_periodic implementation
description:
Phase 1 Epic B: implement wac_periodic cost method by replacing the close-hook stub from s6n with a real body, plus the dispatcher changes that flag mid-period depletions for re-costing.

DEPENDS ON: acct-s6n (closed) — provides transfers_provisional + close_period orchestration + wac_periodic_close_hook stub.
ENABLES: acct-9tw (Epic C: wac_retroactive — reuses provisional infrastructure with different close math), acct-og1 (Epic E: cost_adjustment_retroactive).

LOCKED-IN DESIGN DECISIONS (acct-hlr design memo, 2026-05-01):

D1 — RECEIPTS DON'T NEED FLAGGING. Receipts post the value via caller-asserted amount (qty × po_unit_price for po_receipt; same shape for cycle_count_adj, inventory_adjustment IN, customer_return, to_receipt). They never go through _post_transfers_compute_amount because that dispatcher only fires for depletion-shaped reasons (op_move, scrap, wo_complete, so_ship). The period-close hook can sum value_in / qty_in directly from the transfers table by querying debit_account_id = inv_value_<class>(sku, location, currency) and business_date in period. No flagging needed.

D2 — PROVISIONAL COST FOR DEPLETIONS = RUNNING_AVG. Mid-period depletions on wac_periodic SKUs post at the period-to-date running average — exact same math as wac_perpetual: pool_value / pool_qty read under FOR UPDATE on the value account. Difference vs wac_perpetual: the depletion gets flagged in transfers_provisional with cost_method='wac_periodic' for re-costing at close. Smallest close-time variance and reuses existing wac_perpetual code. Alternate sources (last period close avg, last purchase price, configured value, zero, standard) are tracked as Epic I (acct-cms).

D3 — POOL GRANULARITY = (sku, location, currency). Period avg is computed per inventory pool, not per-SKU globally. Matches industry standard (Oracle, SAP) and our existing partition.

D4 — EMPTY POOL ON DEPLETION = STRICT P0006. Same as wac_perpetual: 'caller must pass p_unit_cost on first IN to seed' OR 'cannot deplete from empty pool'. Negative inventory support is tracked as Epic H (acct-9ij).

D5 — TRANSFERS_PROVISIONAL SCHEMA EXTENSION. Add a  column (NULLABLE for backward-compat with s6n's stub-era rows). The close hook needs qty to compute variance: variance = (final_period_avg - provisional_cost) × qty. Without a qty column on transfers_provisional or on transfers itself, the hook can't reconstruct this. Adding to transfers_provisional is the lighter change.

D6 — CLOSE_HOOK MATH. wac_periodic_close_hook(p_period_id) walks transfers_provisional rows WHERE period_id= AND cost_method='wac_periodic' AND finalized_at IS NULL. For each, derives (sku, location, currency) from the original transfer's debit account, looks up the period's value_in / qty_in receipts to compute final_avg, computes variance = (final_avg - provisional_unit_cost) × qty (provisional_unit_cost = original transfer's amount / qty). Posts variance against variance_wac_period(currency), updates the row's finalized_at + variance_amount + variance_transfer_id.

D7 — ZERO-RECEIPT EDGE CASE. If a period has provisional depletions but ZERO receipts (qty_in = 0), final_avg is undefined. Behavior: hook raises P0020 (new code: wac_periodic_close_no_receipts) with a clear message — operator must either (a) post a cycle_count_adj or inventory_adjustment to bring inventory in for the period, or (b) close with p_force_provisional=TRUE which leaves the un-finalized rows for forensics (per s6n).

D8 — DOCUMENT WORKFLOWS UNTOUCHED IN THIS EPIC. Receipts (po_receipt, etc.) are out of scope — they're Slice A's concern. This epic only changes what happens when a depletion fires on a wac_periodic SKU and what happens at period close.

SUB-ISSUES:
- qfj.1 — Implementation: migration adding transfers_provisional.qty column + dispatcher refactors (compute_amount + post_inventory_adjustment) + real wac_periodic_close_hook body + smoke tests
- qfj.2 — Full test matrix: receive-deplete-close lifecycle, multi-pool, multi-period, zero-receipt edge case, force-bypass through close_period
- qfj.3 — Doc updates: §3.13/§4 design doc additions, db/README error codes (P0020), CLAUDE.md load-bearing decision

NEW ERROR CODE:
- P0020 — wac_periodic_close_no_receipts (close hook can't compute final avg)

ACCEPTANCE:
1. Existing wac_perpetual SKU behavior unchanged.
2. wac_periodic SKU receives 100 units at $5 + 100 at $7, depletes 50 mid-period (provisional cost = running avg at depletion time).
3. close_period(period, actor) runs: hook computes final_avg = (500+700)/200 = 6, posts variance for the depletion against variance_wac_period(USD), marks the row finalized.
4. inv_value reflects the corrected post-close value.
5. Cannot close with un-finalized provisional rows unless p_force_provisional=TRUE (existing s6n gate).

OUT OF SCOPE:
- wac_retroactive (Epic C)
- cost_adjust_retroactive (Epic E)
- Alternate provisional cost sources (Epic I / acct-cms)
- Negative inventory (Epic H / acct-9ij)
- WIP material revaluation across rolls (Epic G / acct-bru — applies to standard cost roll, not WAC)

title: Pivot post_transfers transport to pseudo-sync (shape L) when contention emerges
description:
Phase 0 → Phase 1 transition keeps post_transfers as a sync inline function call (D3 re-resolved 2026-04-30, see CLAUDE.md and consolidated doc Part VII Q3). The deferral is operational, not architectural: realistic Phase 1 workflows (per-document transfers spread across SKUs/locations) don't naturally hit the contention regime where pseudo-sync's advantages are load-bearing.

But shape L's perf advantages ARE wanted — caller p99 547ms vs sync F's 8.25s (15× better under 100-writer contention), throughput median ~1.8× F. The infrastructure (DrainConfig.notify_channel, single-listener dispatcher, drain-tx pg_notify with SQLSTATE payload) is already built and benched in tests/load_outbox_pseudo_sync.rs. Pivoting later is additive, not a foundation rewrite.

This issue tracks the explicit commitment to revisit when triggered.

Triggers — claim this when ANY are observed in Phase 1+ measurement:

1. Caller p99 on a hot transaction path exceeds ~500ms under realistic load.
2. A single account becomes naturally hot — e.g., a global cogs/revenue account taking 1000s of postings/sec, or a single high-traffic AR/AP account.
3. Concurrent writers on a shared lock target exceed ~20 sustained.
4. §14.1 follow-up cost-method workloads (acct-8gg) show contention regressions vs the perf_baseline_v0.md F number.
5. A specific Phase 1 feature (e.g., commodity provisional pricing settlement, period-close batch) inherently generates 100-way contention.

Scope when claimed:
1. Pick the entry point: a single hot path migrated to pseudo-sync, NOT a full system pivot. Probably commodity settlement or period-close — they're naturally batchy and the caller-blocking semantics fit.
2. Wire DrainConfig + listener dispatcher into the application layer (not just a test harness). Owner process supervision, restart semantics.
3. Define the error-propagation contract: notify payload {id, status, sqlstate, error_message?} unwrapped into the caller's error model.
4. Migrate the chosen call site's tests from inline-function-call to async-rendezvous.
5. Re-run perf_baseline F + L on the new schema; verify L still wins by enough to justify the operational cost on this hot path.
6. Document migration playbook for additional call sites.

Reference:
- perf_baseline_v0.md observations 15, 16, 17 (L, M findings) and the Caveats note about ezm's noise re-measurement.
- tests/load_outbox_pseudo_sync.rs (the L test binary).
- tests/common/outbox_worker.rs (DrainConfig.notify_channel).
- ledger_design_consolidated_v0.md Part VII Q3 (re-resolved 2026-04-30).

title: Optimize post_transfers post-WAC hot-path regression (~16% on shape L)
description:
After acct-uxu (migration 0021) added the WAC dispatcher + lock pre-scan
+ branched single/two-pass execution, shape L commit_evps dropped from
2,876 to ~2,428 evps median (3-run, 100 writers x 5 min) — about 16%
regression on the standard path even when no WAC events are in the batch.

This was characterized in real time: a 'fast path' branch was added in
0021 (single-pass when v_has_wac=FALSE, identical body to migration
0019), and a SQL EXISTS short-circuit was added to skip the pre-scan
loop entirely for non-cost-relevant batches. Neither restored full
performance.

Hypotheses for the residual cost (verify with profiling before optimizing):

1. PL/pgSQL plan cache invalidation. The function body is now ~2x larger
   with multiple IF branches; PG's plan cache may behave differently.
   Possible fix: split into two SQL-callable functions with `post_transfers`
   as a thin dispatcher, OR convert hot blocks to dynamic SQL with
   prepared-statement caching.

2. JSONB pass-0 EXISTS query overhead. Even short-circuiting at the
   first match, the SQL EXISTS evaluation itself costs ~30-50us per
   batch. At 60K batches/run that's ~3s = 1% — small but measurable.
   Possible fix: maintain a per-event reason-set bitmap on the JSONB
   input, or skip the check entirely and detect cost-relevant inline.

3. Function-call overhead. _post_transfers_compute_amount is called per
   cost-relevant value-side event in the two-pass path. Each call
   has parameter marshaling cost. Possible fix: inline the standard
   branch directly in post_transfers, keep the helper for non-standard
   only.

4. accounts row-type passing. p_d_acct accounts and p_c_acct accounts
   are passed by value to the helper. PL/pgSQL may copy the entire
   row each call. Possible fix: pass only the fields actually used
   (sku_id, location_id, routing_op, debits_total, credits_total,
   ledger_kind, kind), or pass by id and re-load inside.

5. Two-pass duplicate SELECTs. Pass 1 and pass 2 both SELECT * INTO
   d_acct, c_acct for the same event when WAC is involved. Could
   cache via PERFORM with array build, or restructure to single SELECT
   per event with state passed forward.

Validation:
  - Re-measure shape L (100 x 5min x 3) after each optimization candidate.
  - Target: commit_evps within 5% of pre-WAC 2,876 evps.
  - Conformance + WAC integration tests must continue passing.
  - Doc: update perf_baseline_v0.md "Caveats" section to remove the
    pre-acct-uxu disclaimer once perf is restored.

Why P3: Phase 0 ships with the regression noted in the doc; shape L
remains the throughput peak across the matrix even at 2,428 evps.
Phase 1 may not need this performance back. If a Phase 1 workload
shows post_transfers as the bottleneck, this is the first issue to
claim.

Reference:
  - perf_baseline_v0.md "Caveats" section (post-acct-uxu addendum)
  - Commit 8ca8032 (acct-uxu hot-path optimization that didn't fully
    restore perf)
  - Migration 0021_post_transfers_wac.up.sql (the function to optimize)
notes: Investigation 2026-04-30: re-measured under proper noise rejection (5 samples × 60s × 30s sleep). Pre-WAC (0021 OUT): n=5 median=2247 min=2049 max=2508 spread=20.4%. Post-WAC (0021 IN): n=5 median=2381 min=2179 max=2508 spread=13.8%. Distributions overlap completely (both max at 2508); post-WAC median is 6% HIGHER than pre-WAC. Original '16% regression' (2876 → 2428 from 3×5min) was within noise — the 3-run sample happened to land pre-WAC at a high point and post-WAC at a low point. Conclusion: NO MEASURABLE REGRESSION from acct-uxu. Hot-path optimization not needed. perf_baseline_v0.md Caveats updated; line 750 regression threshold loosened to match observed noise floor. Bench script saved at /tmp/bench_ezm.sh; logs at /tmp/ezm_20260430_161146_pre_wac and /tmp/ezm_20260430_161906_post_wac.

title: Migration: per-location and per-routing-op UK on value accounts
description:
Schema migration to partition value accounts by location and routing_op
where appropriate, per the decision in acct-5re (option b). Pure
schema work — no behavior change, no test coverage of new shapes.
WAC implementation that consumes these new partitions is acct-uxu.

## Schema changes (single migration)

Drop the existing `accounts_value_uk`:
```sql
DROP INDEX accounts_value_uk;
```

Add three replacement indexes:
```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX accounts_value_loc_uk
  ON accounts (kind, sku_id, location_id, currency)
  WHERE ledger_kind = 'value'
    AND kind IN ('inv_value_raw', 'inv_value_fg')
    AND sku_id IS NOT NULL
    AND NOT is_closed;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX accounts_value_wip_uk
  ON accounts (kind, sku_id, routing_op, currency)
  WHERE ledger_kind = 'value'
    AND kind = 'inv_value_wip'
    AND sku_id IS NOT NULL
    AND NOT is_closed;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX accounts_value_sku_uk
  ON accounts (kind, sku_id, currency)
  WHERE ledger_kind = 'value'
    AND kind IN ('price_trueup_inventory', 'price_trueup_cogs', 'price_trueup_wip')
    AND sku_id IS NOT NULL
    AND NOT is_closed;
```

Currency-only kinds (cogs, revenue, cash, ar, ap, variance_*, labor_*, oh_*, fx_revaluation, inv_adj_expense): no UK index needed beyond what's already implicit (they're identified by application logic, not natural keys, since there can be multiple cash accounts in the same currency for different banks/counterparties).

Add NOT NULL constraint reinforcements where applicable:
```sql
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT accounts_inv_value_loc_not_null
  CHECK (
    NOT (kind IN ('inv_value_raw', 'inv_value_fg') AND sku_id IS NOT NULL)
    OR location_id IS NOT NULL
  );

ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT accounts_inv_value_wip_op_not_null
  CHECK (
    kind <> 'inv_value_wip' OR routing_op IS NOT NULL
  );
```

## Fixture updates

`db/fixtures/small/seed.sql` SKU-A value accounts need location_id and routing_op populated:
- `inv_value_raw(SKU-A, MAIN, USD)` (was no location_id)
- `inv_value_wip(SKU-A, op=10, USD)` and `inv_value_wip(SKU-A, op=20, USD)` (was one row, no op)
- `inv_value_fg(SKU-A, MAIN, USD)` (was no location_id)

T5 conformance fixture: cases referencing `inv_value_*` with `sku_code` selectors will need `location_code` or `routing_op` added depending on kind. Audit ~10 cases.

## Code updates

`tests/common/mod.rs` `account_id_for_selector` already handles `location_code` / `routing_op` resolution. May need a small extension to require them for value-side selectors of partitioned kinds.

## Down migration

Reverse: drop the new indexes, drop the CHECK constraints, recreate the original `accounts_value_uk`. Down requires NO data movement because we're tightening, not relaxing — but the down migration ASSUMES no existing rows would violate the looser UK. In Phase 0 with no production data, that's fine.

## Validation

- ci-check.sh passes; new schema digest recorded.
- Full test suite passes.
- T5 conformance: 103+ cases all pass.
- Shape L smoke: no regression (since this is a structural schema change, not a hot path change).

## Estimate

~1 day. Migration (~2 hours) + fixture updates (~2 hours) + conformance audit/fixes (~2 hours) + test verification (~1 hour) + doc cross-references in db/README (~1 hour).

## Reference

- acct-5re (the decision; doc §4.1 already updated)
- Migration 0006 (current accounts_value_uk being replaced)
- acct-uxu (WAC implementation that consumes the new partitions)
close_reason: Migration 0020 partitions value accounts per doc §4.1: inv_value_raw/inv_value_fg by (sku, location, currency); inv_value_wip by (sku, routing_op, currency). CHECK reinforcements ensure required partition columns are populated. Currency-only kinds (cogs/ar/ap/cash/revenue/variance_*) keep their natural-key-free shape. Fixture seed.sql updated: SKU-A now has inv_value_raw(MAIN,USD), inv_value_wip(op=10,USD), inv_value_wip(op=20,USD), inv_value_fg(MAIN,USD). T5 conformance updated: 18 inv_value_* selectors gained location_code or routing_op. Doc §4.1 partition map fixed (struck price_trueup_* — those are transfer reasons, not account kinds). 103 conformance cases pass; full suite green. Schema digest: 7448257a... Commit bf4623b. Unblocks acct-uxu (WAC).

title: Implement WAC cost method (post_transfers dispatcher branch)
description:
Implement the WAC (weighted average cost) branch of the
`_post_transfers_compute_amount` dispatcher. The dispatcher itself is
introduced by acct-0ig; this issue fills in the WAC branch and adds
the lock pre-scan needed to safely read auxiliary accounts.

## Depends on

- **acct-0ig** (refactor + dispatcher scaffold). Without that, there's no branch to fill in.
- **acct-5re** (schema decision: per-location and per-routing-op granularity on value accounts). Without that, WAC's compute formula and lock topology aren't pinned down.

## Scope

1. Fill in the `'wac'` branch of `_post_transfers_compute_amount`:
   - Read the value-side account's balance (already locked under FOR UPDATE — buffer-cache hit).
   - Read the matching qty-side account(s)'s balance(s). Source depends on the schema decision in acct-5re:
     - If acct-5re picks (a) Global WAC: SUM(qty across all stock_available(sku, *) for that SKU).
     - If acct-5re picks (b) Per-location WAC: read stock_available(sku, p_event.location_id).
   - `unit_cost = value_balance / qty_balance`.
   - `RETURN qty * unit_cost`.

2. **Lock pre-scan** in `post_transfers`:
   - Before the main FOR UPDATE, walk events and identify auxiliary accounts WAC needs.
   - Snapshot-read each event's debit/credit accounts (sku_id, location_id, kind).
   - For cost-relevant value-side events with cost_method='wac', look up the matching qty-side account ID(s).
   - Combined SELECT acquires FOR UPDATE in ascending-id order across base + aux IDs (preserves the deadlock-free invariant).

3. **Two-pass execution** is already in place from acct-0ig. WAC's compute branch slots into pass 1.

4. **Lock-set expansion correctness:** if option (a) global WAC is chosen, the function locks N accounts (N = # locations holding the SKU). For multi-location SKUs this could be 10s of accounts per event. Document the implication.

## Tests

1. **WAC happy path** (single-location):
   - Receive 100 units @ \$5 = \$500 value, 100 qty.
   - Receive 100 units @ \$7 = \$700 value, 200 qty total. (Now value pool is \$1,200, qty 200, unit \$6.)
   - Issue 50 units. Function computes amount = 50 * 6 = \$300.
   - Verify: value account drops by \$300, qty drops by 50.

2. **WAC after partial issue** (re-average):
   - Above + receive 50 more @ \$10 = \$500.
   - State before issue: value=\$1,400, qty=200, unit=\$7.
   - Issue 50 units. amount = 50*7 = \$350. Verify.

3. **WAC concurrent issue safety**:
   - Two concurrent batches issuing same SKU. Both must compute pre-batch averages, neither should read mid-mutate state. Property: `final_value/final_qty == avg(unit_cost across both batches' weighted by qty)` — sanity check.
   - Asserts 0 deadlocks.

4. **WAC on zero qty**: qty_balance = 0 → divide-by-zero. Must raise a clean error (P0006-equivalent: cost_unavailable). NOT an unhandled ERROR.

5. **WAC value-side without matching qty account**: edge case. Schema decision in acct-5re may rule this out; otherwise raise P0006.

6. **T5 conformance**: 4-6 new WAC cases.

## Validation

- Re-run shape **L** baseline. WAC path's per-event time should be 0.347 + ~0.1 ms/event = ~0.45 ms/event. If higher, investigate.
- Schema digest changes: yes (function body change). Regen.

## Estimate

~2 days. Function branch (~half day) + lock pre-scan (~half day) + WAC tests (~half day) + T5 cases (~half day). Maybe more if acct-5re picks option (b) and the schema migration is bundled here.

## Open questions

1. **Multi-pool WAC** (per-currency): a SKU with both USD and EUR value accounts — separate pools, separate averages? Yes, by definition (currency is a key). Schema enforces this naturally.

2. **WAC + scrap**: scrap is also cost-relevant. `scrap` debits `inv_adj_expense` (or similar), credits the inventory value account. WAC unit cost at scrap is the same formula — no new branch needed.

3. **WAC + wo_complete**: only meaningful if per-op WIP value accounts exist (acct-5re option b). Otherwise stays raise-P0006.

4. **WAC + op_move**: same as above. Per-op WIP value is required.

## References

- Doc §4.2 (cost method — corrected by acct-0ig)
- Doc §6.2 (WAC formula)
- acct-0ig (refactor introducing the dispatcher)
- acct-5re (schema decision blocking this)
- acct-8gg (lot, FIFO — depends on this for the dispatcher pattern to be tested)
close_reason: WAC implementation landed in migration 0021 with 3 commits (9b9be14 main impl, 8ca8032 hot-path branch, 4553a97 doc). Helper _post_transfers_lookup_qty_account maps value accounts to matching qty accounts; _post_transfers_compute_amount WAC branch implements unit_cost = credit_value_balance / matching_qty_balance, amount = qty * unit_cost. post_transfers refactored: lock pre-scan adds WAC aux qty accounts to FOR UPDATE set; two-pass execution (compute then apply) used when v_has_wac=TRUE; single-pass identical to 0019 used otherwise (fast path). Qty-side gate relaxed for cost_method='wac'; stays for lot/fifo. Tests: 107 conformance cases pass (4 new positive WAC, 5 B6 cases converted to SKU-FIF for negative-test parity); tests/wac_post_transfers.rs adds 3 integration tests (re-average across receipts, concurrent issues serialize without deadlock, zero-qty pool raises P0006). Seed extended with SKU-WAC value accounts + SKU-FIF stock_wip. Schema digest fa24e4c20149ad47eddf77e82a422eaf9843317360f29fbabf9f0c9582764192. Perf: shape L commit_evps regresses ~16% (2,876 -> 2,428) due to two-pass overhead; documented in perf_baseline_v0.md and tracked as acct-ezm. Shape L still beats F=1,274 by 1.91x — remains the matrix throughput peak. Unblocks acct-8gg (lot/FIFO).

title: Schema decision: per-location and per-routing-op granularity on value accounts
description:
Surfaced 2026-04-30 during acct-0ig planning. The schema's value account
model doesn't match the doc's stated granularity, and this mismatch
blocks honest WAC implementation.

## The mismatch

Doc §4.1 states (verbatim):
- 'WIP qty: one account per (parent_sku, routing_op).'
- 'WIP value: one account per (parent_sku, routing_op, currency).'

Schema (`accounts_value_uk` from migration 0006):
```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX accounts_value_uk
  ON accounts (kind, sku_id, currency)
  WHERE ledger_kind = 'value' AND sku_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT is_closed;
```

So the schema enforces ONE value account per (kind, sku, currency) —
NO routing_op, NO location_id. Doc says per (sku, op, currency) for
WIP value. Doc is silent on per-location for stock-value pools, but
standard ERP practice has per-(sku, location) running averages.

## Two concrete consequences

### Consequence A — op_move on value side is a balance no-op

Per migration 0013, `op_move` is in the cost-relevant set, intended to
move WIP value between routing ops. With the current schema, the SAME
`inv_value_wip(sku, USD)` account is debited and credited (because it's
unique per (sku, currency) — no per-op partition). Net balance change: 0.

Confirmed by T5 conformance fixture: A2_op_move_standard_sku and
A3_op_move_chain only post on the QTY side (stock_wip(sku, op)). The
fixture is implicitly skirting this design problem — there's no
test case where op_move actually moves value between ops.

### Consequence B — WAC has nothing to compute against per location

Standard ERP WAC is per (sku, location): each location maintains its
own running average. With current schema, value is global per
(sku, currency). WAC unit cost would have to be:
- value_balance(sku, USD) / SUM(qty across all locations)

That requires every WAC issue to lock all `stock_available(sku, *)`
rows. Across many locations that's a lot of locks per event. And it
sacrifices per-location cost tracking (can't tell which location's
inventory is more expensive on a weighted-avg basis).

## Three options

### Option (a): Global WAC, accept the schema as-is

- Value pool is global per (sku, currency).
- Qty divisor = SUM(stock_available) across all locations.
- WAC issue locks ALL stock_available(sku, *) accounts.
- Per-op WIP value: stays as no-op for op_move; only post on stock_wip(sku, op) qty side. Doc §4.1 wording corrected to match schema reality.
- Pros: no schema change. Works for single-location SKUs (Phase 0 fixture).
- Cons: heavy lock fanout for multi-location. Loses per-location cost.
- Effort: WAC implementation only, no schema migration.

### Option (b): Per-location and per-op value accounts

- Schema migration: extend `accounts_value_uk` to include `location_id` and `routing_op` where relevant. Different value `kind`s have different uniqueness:
  - inv_value_raw, inv_value_fg: per (kind, sku, location, currency) — perhaps location optional → SUM across locations on demand.
  - inv_value_wip: per (kind, sku, routing_op, currency).
  - cogs, ap, ar, cash, revenue, variance_*: per (kind, currency) — no per-sku/loc/op partition.
- WAC reads per-location value pool / per-location qty.
- op_move on value side becomes meaningful: dr inv_value_wip(sku, op_to, USD), cr inv_value_wip(sku, op_from, USD).
- Pros: matches doc §4.1, matches standard ERP practice, simpler WAC.
- Cons: schema migration touching the accounts table; account-creation code needs updating; conformance fixture needs more accounts.
- Effort: schema migration (1 day) + account-creation code updates (0.5 day) + WAC implementation against new schema (1-2 days) + fixture/test updates (1 day).

### Option (c): Hybrid — per-(sku, currency) for value pools, but track per-location qty separately

- Keep value accounts global per (kind, sku, currency).
- Add a per-(sku, location) MOH/cost projection table that computes a per-location implied unit cost on-demand.
- Avoids schema change but adds projection complexity.
- Cons: mostly the same as (a) — projection ≈ summing locks anyway.
- Effort: comparable to (a).

## What we need from this issue

1. Decide between (a), (b), (c) — or surface a fourth option.
2. Update doc §4.1 wording to match the chosen model.
3. If (b): file the schema migration as its own sub-issue (or fold into the WAC implementation issue).
4. Become the explicit blocker on the WAC implementation issue (and downstream cost-method work in acct-8gg).

## Recommendation (not committed — needs user approval)

Option (b). Reasons:
- Matches doc intent.
- Standard ERP semantics; less surprising for future engineers.
- WAC becomes a clean dispatcher branch instead of a multi-row aggregation.
- Schema migration is mechanical (additive, no data loss).
- The conformance fixture is small enough that updating it is bounded work.

But (a) is genuinely defensible if 'this is a single-location-per-SKU
system' is acceptable for the foreseeable future. Most real ERPs are
multi-location, but Phase 0/1 fixtures might not need to be.

## When to claim

Claim before starting WAC implementation. Without this resolved, WAC
will either be implemented against the wrong model (option a/c
masquerading as b) or will be repeatedly half-rewritten as the schema
clarifies.

## References

- Migration 0006 (accounts schema) lines 37-39 (accounts_value_uk index)
- Doc §4.1 (WIP model — granularity claim)
- Doc §6.2 (WAC formula — unit cost = value_balance / qty_on_hand)
- T5 conformance fixture cases A2_op_move_*, A3_op_move_chain (which skirt the value-side problem)
- acct-0ig (the refactor that surfaced this; narrowed to standard-only)
close_reason: Decision: option (b) — value accounts partition by the same dimensions as their qty-side counterparts. Doc §4.1 updated with the explicit partition map (inv_value_raw and inv_value_fg per (sku, location, currency); inv_value_wip per (sku, routing_op, currency); cogs/revenue/cash/ar/ap/variance_* per (currency); price_trueup_* per (sku, currency)). Schema migration that implements the new UKs is filed as acct-nfr, now a prereq of acct-uxu (WAC). Reasons for option (b) over (a)/(c): matches doc §4.1 intent for WIP value, standard ERP per-location WAC semantics, simpler WAC dispatch (no SUM-across-locations hack), no production data exists yet so migration is mechanical. Commit 379e707.

title: Reopen D3 (sync vs async outbox) with shape L's evidence
description:
Phase 0 perf baseline (acct-yjn, 2026-04-30) produced shape L (pseudo-sync via LISTEN/NOTIFY) with results that CONTRADICT D3's load-bearing rationale.

D3's original claim (CLAUDE.md Load-bearing decisions, original wording): 'sync post_transfers is dominant by every measure for sync-required ERP flows; outbox is the right architecture only when caller p99 is the binding constraint AND eventual semantics on the ledger are acceptable.'

Shape L's measurement contradicts this:
- Commit throughput: 2,876 evps vs F's 1,274 evps (2.26x BETTER, not worse)
- Caller end-to-end p99: 547 ms vs F's 8,251 ms (15x BETTER, not equivalent)
- Error semantics: PRESERVED (notify payload carries SQLSTATE on per-row failure)
- Tradeoff: caller must BLOCK on a per-id notify rendezvous (added client complexity vs inline function call)

D3's 'sync is dominant' framing is no longer factually supported. The remaining argument for sync is operational simplicity — caller code is simpler when post_transfers is an inline function call vs a register-listener-then-INSERT-then-await dance.

Scope when claimed:
1. Re-read Part VII Q3's resolution and CLAUDE.md's no-outbox-in-Phase-0 paragraph.
2. Decide: keep Phase 0 as sync (status quo, simplicity wins for foundation), OR pivot to L (throughput wins, complexity manageable).
3. If keep-sync: rewrite the rationale to be about caller-side complexity, NOT throughput. The current text claims throughput superiority that no longer exists.
4. If pivot-to-L: file a Phase 1 epic for the pseudo-sync transport (DrainConfig.notify_channel, listener orchestration, error-propagation contract for caller, document migration impact on existing call sites).
5. Either way: update CLAUDE.md and the consolidated doc Part VII Q3 with the chosen framing + L's evidence link.

Why P3: not blocking Phase 0 work. The decision needs Phase 1 framing to be in flight (so we know what concurrency Phase 1 actually needs); claiming this prematurely re-litigates a settled-for-now decision. But surface it the moment Phase 1 framing reaches a 'how do callers post transfers?' question.

Reference:
- perf_baseline_v0.md observations 15, 16, 17 (L, M findings)
- Commit 297b6f5 (acct-yjn writeup)
- tests/load_outbox_pseudo_sync.rs (the L test binary)
- tests/common/outbox_worker.rs (DrainConfig.notify_channel)
close_reason: Re-resolved: stay sync for now (Phase 0 → Phase 1 entry), pivot to L deferred to Phase 1+ when contention emerges. Original 'sync is dominant by every measure' rationale was wrong — L wins on latency-and-throughput-under-contention. Corrected rationale: operational simplicity for foundation, with explicit commitment to revisit. CLAUDE.md and consolidated doc Part VII Q3 updated. Follow-up tracking issue with explicit revisit triggers filed as acct-c4p.

title: Explore: super-batched outbox drainer (events from N rows merged into one post_transfers call)
description:
Follow-up to acct-tyq, prompted by acct-4fj/acct-epu finding: the naive single-writer drain pattern (one post_transfers call per outbox row) does NOT recover shape B's amortization. post_transfers per-call overhead dominates because shape B's win comes from packing 1000 events INTO one call, not from running 1000 calls in series.

This issue prototypes an alternate worker design: optimistically concatenate events from N pending rows into a SINGLE post_transfers call (the 'super-batch'). On success, mark all N rows committed. On failure, the entire super-batch rolls back; recover by falling back to per-row savepoint mode (current acct-6hm worker) for that specific batch.

Tradeoff:
- Win: single post_transfers call amortizes parsing/planning/lock overhead across all N rows' events. Should approach shape B's 2486 evps.
- Lose: error attribution is coarsened. A P0001 caused by writer X's row poisons writers Y and Z's rows in the same super-batch (those rows roll back via the outer tx, then the fallback per-row pass commits Y/Z but defers X's failure to row-level). Worker becomes more complex.
- Operational: the failure-fallback adds latency for entire super-batches that contain even one bad event. Real workloads are mostly clean, so this is fine — but it warrants measurement.

Acceptance:
- Implement a 'super_batched' variant of the worker (probably tests/common/outbox_worker.rs gets a second drain function or a config flag).
- Run a load test variant (likely tests/load_outbox_super_batch.rs) with same fixture as shape G.
- Headline: did super-batching recover shape B-class throughput? What was the caller-perceived latency profile?
- Updated perf section comparing G (naive) vs G' (super-batch) vs F (sync) vs B (TB-style direct).
- Decision recommendation: should we re-open D3 with this evidence?

Sequencing: P3, gated AFTER acct-tyq writeup (acct-epu) lands so the comparison is concrete.
acceptance_criteria: Super-batched worker variant + load test + comparison writeup. Either recommends D3 reopen or documents why super-batch isn't worth the error-attribution cost.
close_reason: Shape J added to perf_baseline_v0.md. Super-batched outbox drainer (merges events from up to 1000 outbox rows into one post_transfers call): 365 evps committed (2.6× G's 140, but 3.5× less than F's 1274). Caller p99=108ms (76× better than F), per-event 2.8ms (between F's 4.25 and B's 0.37). Closes ~half throughput gap to F via amortization; remaining gap is parallelism not amortization. 0 deadlocks. D3 stands. Committed b6d96f2.

title: acct-tyq sub: load test — shape G (100 writers → outbox → 1 drainer)
description:
New load test binary tests/load_outbox_workload.rs modeled on load_realistic_workload.rs (same 50-SKU × 2-location cross-account spread fixture for fair comparison vs shape F).

Differences from load_realistic_workload:
- Writer task body becomes: INSERT INTO ledger_outbox (events, override_closed_period) VALUES ($1, $2). No post_transfers call from writers.
- Spawn 1 drain worker task (from acct-tyq.2 module) running concurrently with writers.
- Latency instrumentation captures TWO latencies per event:
  - enqueue_us: writer's INSERT round-trip
  - commit_us: enqueue_at → committed_at (read from row after worker drains it; worker stamps committed_at)
  - end_to_end_us = commit_us (ROW.committed_at - enqueue_us'_t0_at_writer_side) — instrumented by writer recording t0, then post-test querying outbox for committed_at and computing diff
- Output extended T4_CSV_HEADER / T4_CSV_VALUES with columns for both latency families.
- Same env vars: T4_DURATION_SECS, T4_WRITERS, T4_EVENTS_MIN/MAX, T4_BENCH_SKUS.
- Track outbox depth over time (sample pending count every 5s) for queue-depth analysis.

Acceptance: test runs to completion under a short (60s) smoke run; emits CSV; outbox is fully drained at end (status='committed' for all enqueued rows except any deliberate failures); depth samples written to log.
acceptance_criteria: Test compiles, 60s smoke run drains cleanly, CSV emitted with both enqueue and commit latency columns.
close_reason: Shape-G load test landed. Smoke run validates infrastructure: writers INSERT, single drain worker, two latency families (enqueue + queue), bounded grace drain with hard_stop fallback, depth sampling. Smoke headline: 366 evps committed vs F's 1274 — confirms naive single-worker is slower than direct sync. Full benchmark in acct-epu. Committed ff5d6b5.

title: acct-tyq sub: outbox drain worker (single-writer, big-batch)
description:
Implement the outbox drain worker logic. Lives in a small Rust module reachable from the load test (likely tests/common/outbox_worker.rs, public to benchmark code). Loop:
1. BEGIN
2. SELECT id, events, override_closed_period FROM ledger_outbox WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT N (configurable, default 1000)
3. For each selected row: call post_transfers(events, override_closed_period). On success → UPDATE SET status='committed', committed_at=now(). On error → UPDATE SET status='failed', error_sqlstate=…, error_text=…, attempt_count=attempt_count+1.
4. COMMIT
5. If 0 rows selected: short sleep (configurable, e.g. 1ms) before next iteration. If >0 rows: loop immediately (drain backlog at full speed).

Single-writer mode (one task/thread driving the loop). The 4-worker variant (acct-tyq.5) is a separate config later.

Lock pattern note: SKIP LOCKED + ORDER BY id ensures progress even if another drainer holds the head row. With single-writer there's no other drainer — but the pattern is right for the multi-worker followup.

No automatic retry — failed rows stay 'failed' until manually re-driven. Benchmark doesn't need retry semantics for the throughput question.

Acceptance: worker drains a seeded outbox of N=10000 rows correctly; row counts by status match expected; happy-path and one-error-row case both observed.
acceptance_criteria: Worker module callable from test; drains 10k seeded rows with correct final status counts.
close_reason: Drain worker module + smoke test landed. 10k rows drained correctly, savepoint per-row isolation works (1 failure with sqlstate 23514, rest committed), terminal counts and committed_at all asserted. Committed b5e0098.

title: acct-tyq sub: ledger_outbox schema migration (0017)
description:
Add migrations 0017_ledger_outbox.up/.down.sql. Table holds enqueued event batches awaiting ledger commit:
- id BIGSERIAL PK
- enqueued_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
- events JSONB NOT NULL  (the array of event objects post_transfers expects)
- override_closed_period BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE
- status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (status IN ('pending','committed','failed'))
- committed_at TIMESTAMPTZ
- error_sqlstate TEXT
- error_text TEXT
- attempt_count INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0

Index for drain pattern: (status, id) WHERE status='pending' — supports SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED ORDER BY id LIMIT N.

Reversible .down.sql drops table. Schema digest will change — acceptable since this lands on a benchmark branch and only ships if benchmark wins.

Acceptance: ci-check.sh passes; up/down round-trip clean; idle table doesn't break existing tests.
acceptance_criteria: 0017 up/down migrations present, ci-check passes, schema digest captured.
close_reason: Migration 0017 added; up/down/redeploy clean via ci-check.sh; full test suite passes with idle table; schema digest 86e24c34. Committed 0676e59.

title: Explore: bounded-queue + LISTEN/NOTIFY pseudo-sync caller pattern
description:
Exploratory follow-up to acct-tyq. acct-tyq benchmarks the canonical async outbox (caller fires-and-forgets, errors surface via row state). This issue covers the alternate flavor we considered but did not benchmark: a bounded in-DB queue where the caller writes a row and waits via LISTEN/NOTIFY (or short polling) for the worker to commit and signal back.

From the caller's perspective this is pseudo-sync — they still block until ledger commit — but execution is decoupled (single-writer worker amortizes commits, callers don't hold per-batch locks). The interesting characterization vs acct-tyq's async outbox:
- Does it preserve sync-style error propagation (caller gets the SQLSTATE) without giving up shape-B-style throughput?
- What's the caller-perceived p99 vs shape F (direct sync) and acct-tyq's async outbox?
- Operational complexity (NOTIFY queue depth, re-arm on missed signals, worker failover) — is it worth it vs just running async outbox?

Not a requirement. File only if acct-tyq's results suggest the throughput-vs-error-semantics tradeoff is real and we want a third data point. Gated AFTER acct-tyq lands.
close_reason: Shape L (pseudo-sync via LISTEN/NOTIFY) is the NEW throughput peak — 2,876 commit-evps (2.26x F, 16% above B, 7.9x J), caller end-to-end p99=547ms (15x better than F). Writers INSERT then BLOCK on a notification matching their row id; drainer super-batches as in J + emits pg_notify per row outcome inside the drain tx. Naturally bounded queue depth (= writer count). Pipelines writer-INSERT and drainer-commit phases, eliminating the 100-way account-FOR-UPDATE contention that limits F. Shape M (busy-poll back-pressure cap=200) characterized as a strict regression vs L on throughput (3x), caller p99 (6.8x), and CPU efficiency (cs/s 5.5x higher). Both shapes documented in perf_baseline_v0.md (shapes L and M, observations 15-17). D3's 'sync post_transfers is dominant' rationale is now contradicted by L's evidence; reopening D3 with L's data is a separate decision (not yet filed). Code: tests/load_outbox_pseudo_sync.rs, tests/load_outbox_back_pressure.rs; DrainConfig.notify_channel option in tests/common/outbox_worker.rs. Commit 297b6f5.

title: Load test: reservation interleaving (reserve_inventory concurrent with post_transfers)
description:
Follow-up to acct-2ey. Today's load test family exercises only post_transfers. Real workloads interleave reserve_inventory() calls — and the reservation flow itself acquires FOR UPDATE on the target stock_available account inside reserve_inventory. So concurrent reserve_inventory + post_transfers traffic against the same (sku, location) pair contends in two ways:

1. The reservation INSERT blocks until it has the stock_available row's lock.
2. post_transfers locks the same row when posting transfers that touch it.

Characterize:
- Mix of (e.g.) 70% post_transfers + 30% reserve_inventory across N writers.
- Throughput, latency, deadlock count.
- Is the two-statement pattern in reserve_inventory() (acct-alq) still safe under high concurrency with post_transfers competing for the same row?

Sequencing: gated AFTER acct-2ey, so the post_transfers-only spread baseline is the comparison point. Likely useful before acct-tyq (outbox vs sync) to characterize what realistic mixed traffic looks like.
close_reason: Shape H added to perf_baseline_v0.md. Mixed qty + reservation traffic at 100 writers (70 posters + 30 reservers): qty throughput -7% vs F (1186 vs 1274 evps) but qty p99 IMPROVES 32% (5.6s vs 8.25s). 724 rps reservation throughput. 0 deadlocks across 660K reservation calls. reserve_inventory PL/pgSQL function (migration 0014) safe under load. Committed 378b63f.

This issue extends the load test family with a value-side workload that exercises USD + EUR concurrently and the value-side per-(currency) lock targets (cash, ar, revenue, ap) as well as per-counterparty subaccounts when those land.

Specifically:
- Per-currency cash/ar/ap/revenue accounts (currently 1 each per currency in fixture) stay hot — that's the realistic case.

Multi-pool ledger composition is roughly additive — pools don't share locks. 50-writer qty subset performs +168% better per-writer than F (100 writers). title: T4 load: scale to spec target (100 writers / 30 min) + perf characterization
description:

This issue is THE Phase-0-baseline producer. Per the 2026-04-29 directive ("establish a baseline on the simplest version of the implementation, before any complexity is added"), it stays narrowly scoped:

title: Doc §3.3: replace single-statement reserve CTE with reserve_inventory() function
description:
The reserve example in ledger_design_consolidated_v0.md §3.3 (around lines 856-872) shows a single CTE+INSERT pattern that is unsafe under concurrent reservers in READ COMMITTED:

    WITH avail AS (
      SELECT a.id,
        (a.debits_total - a.credits_total) - COALESCE((
          SELECT SUM(qty) FROM inventory_reservations r
          WHERE r.sku_id = a.sku_id AND r.location_id = a.location_id AND r.status = 'active'
        ), 0) AS qty_promisable
      FROM accounts a
      WHERE a.kind = 'stock_available' AND a.sku_id = $sku AND a.location_id = $loc
      FOR UPDATE
    )
    INSERT INTO inventory_reservations ...
    SELECT ... FROM avail WHERE qty_promisable >= $qty
    RETURNING id;

Postgres takes one snapshot per command. The FOR UPDATE on the accounts row correctly serializes contenders, but the SUM subquery inherits the snapshot taken at command start — before the FOR UPDATE wait — so each waiter sees the same pre-contention reservations view and over-promises. Demonstrated by the T3 reserve_concurrency test (acct-93b.18); on-hand=10 with 5 concurrent 3-unit requests over-promised to 12.

Fix already shipped in code: migration 0014_reserve_inventory.up.sql defines a PL/pgSQL function reserve_inventory() that uses two separate SQL statements (FOR UPDATE; then SELECT promisable). Each PL/pgSQL statement takes its own snapshot in READ COMMITTED, so the SELECT after the wait sees the prior winner's INSERT. Test now passes deterministically with successes=3.

Action for this issue: update ledger_design_consolidated_v0.md §3.3 to:
  (1) note the snapshot-semantics gotcha,
  (2) replace the CTE example with reserve_inventory() invocation,
  (3) keep the allocate / cancel / expire UPDATE statements as-is (those are single-row UPDATEs guarded by status='active' and don't have the same issue).

Priority 3 (post-Phase-0): code is correct, only the doc text is stale. No callers exist yet.
close_reason: Doc §3.3 updated: replaced single-statement CTE+INSERT with reserve_inventory() function call. Kept the unsafe CTE as a 'DO NOT USE' anti-example with the READ COMMITTED snapshot-semantics explanation so the bug isn't regenerated. References migration 0014 and the T3 test. Allocate/Cancel/Expire blocks unchanged. Committed a90eca2.

title: post_transfers: switch to function-computed amount for cost-relevant reasons (Option B)
description:
**Narrowed scope (2026-04-30, after schema review):** REFACTOR ONLY.
Move 'amount' computation into the function on the **standard path only**.
WAC, lot, FIFO branches scaffolded with RAISE P0006 + explicit TODO
comments referencing their downstream issues. WAC implementation is
filed separately because it requires schema decisions that are
out-of-scope here.

## What this issue does

1. New helper `_post_transfers_compute_amount(p_event, p_d_acct, p_c_acct, p_cost_method) RETURNS BIGINT`. Dispatcher with branches:
   - `'standard'`: `RETURN qty * skus.standard_cost`. Real, working.
   - `'wac'`: `RAISE P0006 'wac_not_implemented; tracked as <new WAC issue>'`.
   - `'lot'`: `RAISE P0006 'lot_not_implemented; tracked as acct-8gg + lot infra'`.
   - `'fifo'`: `RAISE P0006 'fifo_not_implemented; tracked as acct-8gg + lot infra'`.

2. Refactor `post_transfers` to **two-pass** structure:
   - Pass 1 (compute): for each event, compute `amount[i]` from either `qty` (cost-relevant value-side) or the supplied `amount` (everything else).
   - Pass 2 (validate + apply): all 8 invariants checked per-event in order; idempotency check; UPDATE accounts; INSERT transfers.
   - Why two-pass: locks WAC's pre-batch-balance invariant in for the future. The compute pass reads balances; the apply pass mutates them. Even though the standard path doesn't need pre-batch balances, structuring the code two-pass NOW means WAC can drop in as a single dispatcher branch later — no further function refactor required.

3. Bifurcate input contract:
   - Cost-relevant reasons (`op_move`, `scrap`, `wo_complete`, `so_ship`) on **value-ledger events**: caller MUST send `qty`, function computes `amount`. Caller's `amount` (if supplied) is ignored.
   - Same reasons on **qty-ledger events**: caller still sends `amount` (= qty by convention). Unchanged.
   - All other reasons: caller sends `amount`. Unchanged.

4. Update T5 conformance fixture (~22 cost-relevant cases): replace `"amount": N` with `"qty": N/standard_cost` for value-side events of cost-relevant reasons.

5. Update T1/T2/T3 Rust tests touching cost-relevant reasons (handful).

6. Update db/README.md "Write path" section to document the bifurcated input shape.

7. Migration 0019: new helpers + new `post_transfers` body. Down: revert to 0013.

8. Schema digest regen via ci-check.sh.

## What this issue does NOT do

- Implement WAC. Tracked separately as the new WAC implementation issue.
- Implement lot or FIFO. Tracked as `acct-8gg`, which depends on lot infrastructure.
- Touch schema. The lock pre-scan needed for WAC is part of the WAC issue, not this one. Standard path doesn't need it.

## Validation

- Re-run shape **L** baseline. Per-event time should stay 0.347 ± 0.02 ms (zero perf change on standard path).
- T5 conformance: all 100 cases pass (with input-shape updates).
- All existing T1/T2/T3 tests pass.

## Why narrow

The original issue text suggested this was a hard prereq for non-standard cost methods. True. But the schema model for value accounts (per `(sku, currency)`, NO location_id, NO routing_op — see `accounts_value_uk`) doesn't match doc §4.1's claimed `(parent_sku, routing_op, currency)` granularity. Implementing WAC against the current schema requires either (a) global WAC (sum qty across all locations — heavy), (b) schema change (add location_id + routing_op to value UK), or (c) accept single-location simplification (fragile). That decision is out-of-scope here; tracked as a separate sub-issue.

This issue can land **independently** and unblocks the dispatcher pattern. The non-standard method issues then become "fill in the dispatcher branch + add helper queries."

## Estimate

~1-1.5 days. Function rewrite (~half day) + test updates (~half day) + conformance (~half day mechanical).

## Reference

- perf_baseline_v0.md observation 15-17 (shape L baseline for validation)
- Migration 0013 (current Option A code)
- Doc §4.1 (WIP grain, may need wording fix in same PR — see schema sub-issue)
- Doc §4.2 (cost method, the "external cost engine" wording is wrong per user 2026-04-30 — corrected in same PR)
close_reason: Migration 0019 lands the function-computed-amount refactor on the standard path. Dispatcher helper _post_transfers_compute_amount with branches for standard (real), wac/lot/fifo (RAISE P0006 with TODO refs to acct-uxu / acct-8gg). Bifurcated input contract: value-ledger events of cost-relevant reasons (op_move, scrap, wo_complete, so_ship) carry qty; function computes amount. Qty-side gate preserved from 0013. Single-pass execution (two-pass refactor folded into acct-uxu where pre-batch-balances are actually needed). 103 conformance cases pass (3 new: A11b/A11c/B6b). Shape L smoke shows no perf regression on standard path. Doc §4.2 updated (struck 'external cost engine'). Schema digest: 9dd9a096... Commit 68cf621.

title: periods: prevent overlapping date ranges (EXCLUDE USING gist)
description:
Latent foot-gun uncovered while implementing W1 (post_transfers / acct-93b.14). The 'periods' table has no constraint preventing two rows with overlapping [opens_at, closes_at] ranges. post_transfers' period lookup is:

  SELECT id, closed_at INTO v_period_id, v_period_closed
    FROM periods
   WHERE opens_at <= v_business_date AND closes_at >= v_business_date;

If two periods overlap, this query returns >1 rows. Per PL/pgSQL semantics, SELECT INTO (without STRICT) silently picks the first row from the plan — which is NOT deterministic. Posts with business_date in the overlap window would land in an arbitrarily-chosen period.

Why latent: Phase 0 fixture (acct-93b.16 / T1) seeds non-overlapping periods. Production setups using a normal monthly/quarterly cadence won't trip it either. But there's no DB-level guarantee, and the failure mode (silent mis-period assignment) is hard to spot.

Fix:

  ALTER TABLE periods
    ADD CONSTRAINT periods_no_overlap
    EXCLUDE USING gist (
      daterange(opens_at, closes_at, '[]') WITH &&
    );

Notes:
- Uses inclusive [opens_at, closes_at] daterange to match post_transfers' inclusive lookup semantics.
- GiST supports range types natively in PG 18; btree_gist extension is NOT required (only needed when mixing range types with scalar types in the same EXCLUDE constraint).
- Down migration drops the constraint.

Verification:
- Insert two non-overlapping periods -> succeeds.
- Insert a period that overlaps an existing one -> 23P01 (exclusion_violation).
- Adjacent periods (e.g., 2026-04-01..2026-04-30 and 2026-05-01..2026-05-31) MUST be allowed; verify with explicit insert.

Out of scope: changing post_transfers to use STRICT (would surface the issue at runtime instead of preventing it at INSERT time). The constraint is the right layer.
close_reason: Migration 0018 adds EXCLUDE constraint on periods using gist + inclusive daterange. 5-case integration test covers adjacent (legal), midpoint overlap (23P01), full-contain both directions (23P01), and 1-day boundary overlap (23P01). Schema digest captured; ci-check passes; full suite green. Committed 6bf313b.

title: Convert transfers to time partitioning + idempotency_keys side table
description:
Phase 0 ships transfers as a non-partitioned table with idempotency_key UNIQUE directly on the column (decided when L3 / acct-93b.11 was implemented). Reason: doc §1.2 spec is internally inconsistent — PARTITION BY RANGE (posted_at) + UNIQUE (idempotency_key) is impossible in Postgres because unique constraints on partitioned tables must include every partition-key column. Phase 0 chose the simpler resolution since no perf baseline yet justifies partitioning.

This issue covers the eventual conversion when the Part IV §14.1 exploratory baseline produces evidence that partitioning is needed.

Scope:
1. Create 'idempotency_keys' table (key UUID PK, transfer_id BIGINT, posted_at TIMESTAMPTZ, ...). Non-partitioned.
2. Rewrite post_transfers idempotency check to INSERT into idempotency_keys first; unique violation -> short-circuit with 'exists' for that event.
3. Convert transfers to PARTITION BY RANGE (posted_at) with PRIMARY KEY (id, posted_at). Two viable migration patterns: rename + recreate + insert-select, or attach existing as default partition then split. Pick based on data volume at conversion time.
4. Drop transfers.idempotency_key UNIQUE; column stays as a non-unique reference.
5. Document partition-rotation runbook (originally noted as a separate sub-issue when L3 was scoped — folded in here).
6. Migrate all 6 indexes from §1.2 to the partitioned shape.

Gate: Part IV §14.1 exploratory baseline must show partitioning is justified by query/archival patterns. Until then, do not start.
notes:
acct-1s6r evidence (2026-05-11): Trigger NOT fired. End-to-end Slice A+B+C mixed workload at 32 writers × 600s:
- posting_lines grew 200 → 239298 rows / 115.6 MB in 600s
- Sustained rate = 398 rows/s / 0.19 MB/s
- Annualized (24/7 sustained): ~12.6 M rows/year / ~16.6 GB/year
- Well within single-table comfort zone; query plans not degraded
Re-evaluate when:
- Running rate suggests >100 GB/year, OR
- Query plan shows seq-scan regression on the existing 6 indexes, OR
- Cold-row archival becomes operationally required
See perf_baseline_v2.md for full numbers.

title: Add cost methods beyond standard (WAC, FIFO, lot-based)
description:
Phase 0 implements only the 'standard' cost method, with skus.cost_method as a dispatch hook in W2 (D4 closure). 'wac', 'fifo', and 'lot' branches raise P0006 ('cost_method_not_implemented').

Future work:

WAC (likely Phase 1):
- Adds the read-then-write-under-FOR UPDATE pattern that Part IV §3.4 already documents.
- Schema cost: zero — uses existing value/qty accounts. Unit cost = value / NULLIF(qty, 0).
- Test cost: order-dependent fixtures (T5 conformance must encode prior receipt history).

FIFO (likely Phase 2):
- Schema cost: new inventory_cost_layers(sku_id, location_id, qty_remaining, unit_cost, received_at, ...) table.
- Consumption walks oldest layer first; partial consumption splits a layer.
- Test cost: layer-state-dependent fixtures.

Lot-based (likely Phase 2):
- Schema cost: lot_id on receipts and consumption events; new lots(id, sku_id, received_at, unit_cost, ...) table.
- Application layer must surface lot selection at consumption time; this is a bigger feature than just cost.

Decision criteria for which method to add first: driven by actual workload mix uncovered during §14.1 exploratory perf testing and customer/operator demand. Split into per-method issues when prioritized.
notes: 2026-05-08 update: FIFO portion shipped under acct-cbss epic. cost_method='fifo' is now functional via post_posting_lines (mig 0031 cost_layers schema, mig 0032 dispatcher, mig 0033 recon check #8, property_fifo_consistency.rs). Wrapper integration remains open (post_po_receipt / post_so_ship / post_inventory_adjustment / rm_issue_to_wo still raise P0006 at their own gates). Lot portion under acct-uze (E2). Catch-weight scope drift on acct-0kz (E3 Serial) still to surface to user. acct-8gg umbrella stays open until all three (FIFO/Lot/Serial) are wrapper-complete.

title: Benchmark async outbox vs synchronous post_transfers
description:
Phase 0 commits to calling post_transfers synchronously inside the same Postgres transaction as document writes (D3 closed with this default). The optional ledger_outbox pattern (Part IV §1.8) was deferred because the choice is fundamentally a perf question that's hard to answer without real workload data.

Once §14.1 exploratory testing produces a perf baseline on the synchronous path, evaluate whether an async outbox + worker would meaningfully improve write latency or throughput under the actual workload mix. Compare:
- p50 / p95 / p99 latency of document-write-then-post under sync vs outbox+worker
- max sustained TPS for each
- behavior under reservation-heavy and op_move-heavy mixes
- failure modes (worker lag, txn-vs-eventual semantics)

Decision criteria: only adopt outbox if it shows a clear win at expected v1 TPS, or if external integrations (search index, audit sink) make eventual delivery valuable independent of latency.

Depends on: §14.1 exploratory perf baseline (separate plan).
notes: Spawned from acct-93b.3 (D3) closure on 2026-04-27.
close_reason: Shape G characterized + writeup landed in perf_baseline_v0.md. Headline: naive outbox is 9× slower than F on commit throughput (140 vs 1274 evps) but 62× better on caller p99 (133ms vs 8.25s). End-to-end caller latency dominated by queue residency (186s p50). D3 stands. Super-batch variant filed as acct-hbg as the gate to reopen D3. CLAUDE.md + bd memory updated. Committed f88fd0b.

title: Capacity gate slot reservation in xact_pre_commit (defer or close as covered by acct-3ee2)
description:
Carved out of acct-dav7 (external review item #6).

Current xact_pre_commit projects capacity as 'current_occupied + my_new_keys > N_BUCKETS → error'. Race window: between projection and commit-time insert_new_seeded, peer backends can fill slots and push us over. The proposed tightening reserves slots via OCCUPIED_COUNT.fetch_add(new_inserts) in pre_commit and decrements on insert_new_seeded failure.

WHY DEFERRED:
1. acct-3ee2 (M10.C1) already handles the race correctly: insert_new_seeded returns -1 sentinel on full; pgrx::warning! logged; LEDGER_SHMEM_INSERT_FAILURES counted; recon surfaces the drift. No correctness hole.
2. Behavioral change: backends hold capacity reservations across pre_commit → commit gap. Other backends see lower available capacity than would actually exist if all reservations released. Pessimistic accounting regression for unmeasured benefit.
3. Touches the commit-time correctness path — not 'polish'.

WHEN TO REVISIT:
- If LEDGER_SHMEM_INSERT_FAILURES counter ever fires under normal load (currently always 0).
- If hash table fill ratio gets high enough that the race window matters (currently 16384 buckets, well under-subscribed at typical workloads).
- If a future caller has a workload pattern with many large-new-key batches racing for the last slots.

ACCEPTANCE if revisited:
- Slot reservation in xact_pre_commit; decrement on insert_new_seeded failure path; both error-case AND -1-sentinel paths handled.
- Test probe: N concurrent backends each pre-staging M new keys with shmem near capacity; verify (a) one backend's commit succeeds, others get clean ERROR at pre_commit (not -1 sentinel at xact_commit), (b) OCCUPIED_COUNT settles to actual cell count post-quiescence.
- Bench: confirm no throughput regression on the multi-writer fan-in shape (capacity check is per-pre_commit, not per-apply).

OUT OF SCOPE for this issue: hash table resizing, capacity-reuse on cell-deletion (there is no deletion — see Bucket struct doc), multi-database capacity sharing.

title: Extension scope boundaries — additional surfaces + non-extension levers
description:
Sub-issue of acct-togd. Catalog of extension surfaces not in v1 + things the extension explicitly will NOT help with. Complements acct-1oad (future research) by sharpening the v1 scope boundary.

## Additional extension surfaces worth considering

### S1 — Native post_batch via heap_multi_insert

Today the batch API does N INSERTs in one txn. PG's COPY uses heap_multi_insert for bulk; we should too. Wins:
- Single heap-extension lock acquisition vs N
- Single WAL record covering N tuples (or fewer records)
- Better page-level locality
Estimate: 30-50% additional lift on top of v1 batch path. Composable with acct-sw4i shmem rollup.

### S2 — Lock-free idempotency check

UUID idempotency_key UNIQUE B-tree pages get hot across writers under high concurrency (even with random UUIDs, the rightmost pages cluster). Replace with:
- Cuckoo or Bloom filter in shmem (false-positive only on the negative branch — safe)
- Fall back to UNIQUE B-tree lookup only on positive hit
- bgworker maintains the filter from B-tree state

### S3 — Per-backend hot-account write cache

Top-K most-touched accounts get a backend-local accumulator that batches into shmem rollup at txn commit. Reduces shmem hash contention for the small set of accounts taking 80% of writes. Requires careful handling of rollback semantics (cache must be flushed on abort).

### S4 — Native dispatcher body

Today _post_posting_lines_apply_event is plpgsql with switch-on-reason dispatch. Even when each cost-method strategy is native (acct-fngj), the orchestrator pays plpgsql overhead per posting_line. Rewriting the orchestrator in C reduces that to function-call overhead.

### S5 — Composite type for apply_event tuples

Bundle (account, period, currency, ledger_kind, amount, qty) into one passed struct; reduces shmem hash key compute from 6 fields to 1.

### S6 — Native batch validation

Today validation (account exists, period open, amount sign matches account kind) happens in plpgsql per-row inside the apply loop. Native bulk validation could pre-scan a batch in one pass.

## What the extension WILL NOT help with

Tracked here so we don't accidentally scope the extension to solve these:

### N1 — WAL fsync throughput
Hardware + PG conf (commit_delay, wal_compression, synchronous_commit, max_wal_size). Out of extension scope. See acct-1vo7.

### N2 — Buffer pool thrashing  
shared_buffers sizing + working set. Out of extension scope. See acct-1vo7.

### N3 — Connection/process overhead per backend
pgbouncer transaction pooling. Out of extension scope.

### N4 — Plan parsing/binding
Prepared statements (libpq feature). Client-side concern.

### N5 — Network RTT / TLS overhead
Orthogonal to PG entirely.

### N6 — Hot-account FOR UPDATE serialization
acct-slhp sharded balances. Extension shmem rollup eliminates the UPDATE but not the logical 'this account must agree across writers' constraint when readers depend on monotonic balance. Sharding splits the constraint across buckets.

### N7 — MVCC bloat on shadow accounts.balance
Autovacuum tuning; or drop the shadow once we trust shmem rollup. The 'shadow vs replace' decision in acct-sw4i affects whether this matters.

### N8 — Disk IOPS / bandwidth ceiling
Hardware. Sustained throughput ultimately bounded by what the device can sustain.

### N9 — Cross-transaction coordination (SERIALIZABLE)
acct-zroo investigation. The predicate-lock SSI validator has overhead at high tx rates.

### N10 — Catalog locks (relation extension, page split)
heap_multi_insert (S1) mitigates extension-lock contention. Page splits on hot indexes are a B-tree property; mitigated by hash-bucket alternatives (acct-1oad R4) not extension code.

### N11 — B-tree page contention on time-ordered indexes
UUIDv7-default idempotency_key (we use random) and BIGSERIAL id both hit the rightmost B-tree page hard under concurrent writers. Hash-bucket index or partitioning needed; see acct-1oad R4.

### N12 — Replication lag
If streaming replicas exist, WAL apply lag is a hardware + replica config concern. Out of extension scope.

### N13 — TOAST overhead for large columns
posting_line_sources, notes columns >2KB toast. Extension doesn't change storage; if it became a bottleneck, redesign storage (R1 catalog).

### N14 — JIT compilation cost
jit_above_cost = 100000 (default). Hot wrapper plans may JIT. Extension functions in Rust don't need JIT. Audit jit costs after extension lands; may want jit=off for ledger hot path.

### N15 — Stats collector / pg_stat_statements overhead
track_* settings add cost. Acceptable for observability but bound by config not code.

## Why a catalog issue

Memo to future-us so v1 scope doesn't drift to address N-items it can't solve, and S-items have a place to be tracked when they surface as bottlenecks during v1 build.

title: Future research catalog — beyond v1 ledger extension
description:
Research/catalog issue under acct-togd. Captures directions surfaced during v1 design but out of v1 scope.

## R1 — Custom Table Access Method for closed periods

Columnar storage, no MVCC headers, BRIN-only access. OUT of v1 scope per user direction 2026-05-12 (closed-period reads are batched analytics, not critical path). Reconsider when batched-analytics workload shape is concrete (e.g., reporting service hits posting_lines aggregation at scale). Could prototype as PG18 columnar via Citus-style approach.

## R2 — Custom aggregates: parallel-safe SUM by (account, period)

Today: SUM(posting_lines.amount WHERE ...) GROUP BY ... — Postgres parallel-aggregate plan works but per-row decoding is generic. Extension-provided aggregate could declare ledger-specific fastpath. Wins only matter for analytics queries; complementary to R1.

## R3 — bgworker-driven reconciliation

Move run_daily_reconciliation from pg_cron + plpgsql to bgworker + C, with shmem-resident state for hot checks. Pays off if recon walltime becomes a bottleneck for daily ops or if real-time recon signal is wanted.

## R4 — Custom index types tuned for our patterns

- Idempotency-key UNIQUE: random UUID B-tree pages get hot across writers. Hash-bucket index reduces cross-writer contention.
- (account_id, period_id) lookup: extension-provided dense index keyed on rollup hash key, refreshed by bgworker.

Wins are post-shmem-rollup; reconsider after acct-sw4i lands.

## R5 — WAL-level optimizations for ledger-shape records

Ledger posting_lines are small + structured + similar. Custom WAL record type for posting_lines INSERT could:
- Pack 8-16 posting_lines per WAL record (vs one per INSERT)
- Delta-encode account_id / period_id / amount within the pack

PG 18 LZ4 WAL compression captures most of this; specifics matter only at >MB/s sustained WAL.

## R6 — Sharded balances composability

acct-slhp explores per-bucket account splits to break hot-account FOR UPDATE serialization. With shmem rollup (acct-sw4i) the FOR UPDATE goes away entirely, so sharded-balances becomes a write-distribution question, not a contention-relief question. Re-evaluate the sharding shape after shmem rollup ships.

## R7 — pgrx ergonomics audit

First-extension lessons: which PG APIs are stable enough; which are footguns; build/deploy story for a customer-installable extension. Captures the 'we built one, what would we do differently' knowledge.

## R8 — Multi-tenant extension considerations

v1 is single-database. If we ever go multi-tenant, shmem allocation per-tenant + cross-tenant FK isolation becomes a real design question. Out of scope until multi-tenant ambitions surface (synthesis §11.3 open question).

## R9 — rational_t storage in posting_lines.amount

If acct-es0k surfaces drift detectable on the property corpus, consider whether posting_lines.amount itself should become rational_t (16-byte storage) or stay BIGINT with rational_t only as in-flight arithmetic. Storage shift is a schema migration; arithmetic shift is purely extension-scope.

## R10 — Frozen-period balance compression

Once a period closes, its (account, period) rollup cell is immutable. Compress the rollup table per closed-period partition with PG 18 native compression or extension-managed columnar slabs. Complementary to R1 (R1 compresses posting_lines; R10 compresses the rollup).

## Why a catalog issue

Memo to future-us so v1 doesn't get scope-creeped and so we have a place to file related followups as they surface during v1 build.

title: PoC: diagnose batch=1/10 bimodality (run-to-run throughput alternates fast/slow)
description: At small batch sizes (P3 batch=1: runs 1/3/5 = ~1,400 tps; runs 2/4 = ~2,200 tps), throughput alternates. Suspect autovacuum or WAL checkpoint cycle aligning with the 60s-run / 30s-gap pattern. Investigate via pg_stat_bgwriter, pg_stat_io, autovacuum logs. If real, propose a measurement-stability fix (e.g., run vacuum/checkpoint before each replicate; warmup interval after gap). Doesn't change the headline P3/P4 numbers but tightens future-measurement IQR.

title: PoC: COPY FROM STDIN vs multi-row INSERT for batch posting_lines write
description: PG COPY is generally faster than multi-row INSERT for bulk loading (less plan overhead, more efficient WAL granularity). Measure whether the batch API would gain ~10-25% by using COPY internally (via SPI BinaryCopyOut or libpq COPY protocol from the Rust caller). Trade-off: complexity vs throughput. May only be worthwhile at batch=8000+.

title: Reaffirm Tier-2 WASM rules engine out-of-scope decision
description:
The ledger-architecture proposal advocates a two-tier rules engine: Tier 1 configuration-driven (which our cost_method_strategies + close_hooks registries align with) + Tier 2 WASM modules for customer-deployed sandboxed customization. Tier 2 is explicitly out-of-scope for this project (single-tenant; plpgsql IS the customization surface; tier-2 testing infrastructure is '30-50% of the work of building tier 2' per the proposal §3.3.5). Capture this as a load-bearing decision so future architectural-research cycles don't re-ask the question.

Per research/architecture-synthesis.md §8.2 (what we will not adopt — WASM tier rationale), §11.3 (multi-tenant open question).
design: Pure doc work. Decision is conditional on remaining single-tenant; if multi-tenant ambitions emerge later, this gets revisited (§11.3 open question). Until then, plpgsql strategy registry (mig 0094) plays the customization role and is sufficient.
acceptance_criteria: (1) Paragraph added to CLAUDE.md 'Load-bearing design decisions' section OR ledger_design_consolidated_v0.md Part IV reaffirming Tier-2 WASM is not in scope. (2) Cite proposal §3.3 (host API surface, resource limits, testing infrastructure) and §3.5 (critical analysis — multi-quarter engineering cost). (3) Cite proposal's own §3.5 caveat: 'some platforms will be better served by a simpler approach (configuration only)'. (4) Cross-reference research/architecture-synthesis.md §8.2.
